# Propensity Score Methods {#sec-w6}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, students should be able to:

1. Define the propensity score $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$ and explain why it is a *balancing score*.
2. State and prove the Balancing Property ($T \indep X \mid \pi(X)$); prove that conditional exchangeability given $X$ transfers to any balancing score $b(X)$, and explain separately why positivity transfers from $X$ to $b(X)$ (the Propensity Score Theorem).
3. Use the identification formula through the score correctly: stratify on the estimated score (subclassification), and explain why regressing $Y$ on $T$ and $\pi(X)$ does not in general estimate the ATE.
4. Select covariates for the propensity model on causal grounds, weighing the bias of omitting a confounder against the variance of including an unnecessary variable, estimate the score (logistic regression, machine learning), and evaluate the fitted design through balance and overlap diagnostics rather than treatment-prediction accuracy.
5. Derive the IPW identification formula for the ATE, prove the weighted-balance identities, and explain why the Horvitz--Thompson and Hájek estimators differ.
6. Explain why IPW with a well-estimated score can be *more* precise than IPW with the true score, as a projection on the likelihood score vector, and estimate the resulting variance.
7. Explain how IPW estimators can target either the ATE or the ATT depending on the weighting scheme, how the nearest-neighbor matching estimator presented in this chapter targets the ATT, and why matching can tolerate misspecifications of the score that generally bias IPW.
8. Define a prognostic score, state and prove the Prognostic Score Theorem as the mirror image of the Propensity Score Theorem, and explain where the mirror breaks.
9. Distinguish *positivity* (weak overlap) from *strong overlap*, describe the practical consequences of near-violations, and explain the estimand consequences of trimming and re-targeting --- and why clipping the score is neither.
10. (Advanced) Derive the calibration loss of @tan2020regularized as the dual of the shifted Kullback--Leibler calibration problem of @wang2025information, derive its ATT counterpart (entropy balancing), and state what exact covariate balance delivers when the score model is wrong.
11. Articulate the fundamental limitation of propensity-score methods --- the unconfoundedness assumption --- and explain why this motivates instrumental variables (Chapter 7).
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Reading Guide

This chapter can be read at two depths. **First reading**: the curse-of-dimensionality motivation; the balancing property and the *statements* of @lem-coarsest and @thm-ps; the running example and subclassification (@sec-w6-subclassification); the whole of the design-stage material --- covariate selection (@sec-w6-covariate-selection), balance versus prediction, diagnostics (@sec-w6-balance-diagnostics), and the workflow (@sec-w6-design-workflow); the matching and IPW estimator definitions with the weighted-balance identities (@lem-weighted-balance), the definition of a prognostic score and the comparison of @tbl-mirror, and the shift identity (@sec-w6-ht-hajek); positivity, trimming, and re-targeting; and the lab's headline lessons (ATE vs. ATT targeting, Hájek vs. Horvitz--Thompson, behavior under misspecification). **Second reading**: the general-balancing-score proof of @thm-ps; the nonstandard-inference remark for matching; the proofs of @lem-prog-coarsest and @thm-prognostic; the estimated-score efficiency result (@sec-w6-estimated-score) and its variance estimators; the calibration-loss derivation (@sec-w6-calibration); and the level-versus-shape decomposition of the misspecification bias in Part 2 of the lab.
:::

## Motivation: The Curse of Dimensionality {#sec-w6-motivation}

Chapter 5 established that under consistency, conditional exchangeability, positivity, and integrability, the ATE is identified by the back-door adjustment formula, and developed three estimation strategies: regression adjustment, standardization, and stratification. All three require, in practice, that we condition on a covariate vector $X$. When $X$ is low-dimensional, this is feasible. When $X$ has many components, it is not.

**The problem.** Stratification requires cells $\{X = x\}$ to contain both treated and control units. With $p$ binary covariates, there are $2^p$ cells. With $p = 10$, that is 1024 cells --- far more than most datasets can support. Regression adjustment avoids the cell-count problem but requires a correctly specified model for $\E[Y \mid T, X]$, which becomes harder to specify reliably as $p$ grows.

**The solution.** @rosenbaum1983central showed that it is sufficient to condition on a single scalar function of $X$: the *propensity score* $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$. The propensity score reduces the adjustment dimension without changing the identified estimand, provided unconfoundedness and positivity hold. Identification power is preserved; finite-sample efficiency, covariate balance, and robustness to model misspecification, however, depend on how well the score is estimated and how it is used in the downstream estimator.

::: {#exm-running}
## A Running Example: Four Cells, Three Propensity Values

Throughout the chapter we return to an idealized population of $N = 1{,}000$ units with two binary covariates $X = (X_1, X_2)$. Read the proportions in the table as probabilities and $\mu(t,x) = \E\{Y(t) \mid X = x\}$ as population conditional means; under ignorability, $\mu(t,x) = \E(Y \mid T{=}t, X{=}x)$.

| $x=(x_1,x_2)$ | $N_x$ | $N_{1x}$ | $N_{0x}$ | $\pi(x)$ | $\mu(1,x)$ | $\mu(0,x)$ | $\tau(x)$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $(0,0)$ | 400 | 80 | 320 | 0.2 | 5 | 3 | 2 |
| $(1,0)$ | 200 | 100 | 100 | 0.5 | 9 | 6 | 3 |
| $(0,1)$ | 200 | 100 | 100 | 0.5 | 7 | 6 | 1 |
| $(1,1)$ | 200 | 160 | 40 | 0.8 | 12 | 8 | 4 |

The targets are $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \sum_x P(x)\tau(x) = 2.4$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = \sum_x P(x \mid T{=}1)\tau(x) = 30/11 \approx 2.73$, while the naive comparison of arm means is $\bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0 = 8.91 - 4.43 = 4.48$: treated units sit in cells with large $\mu$. Four cells, but only three values of $\pi$: the cells $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ share $\pi = 0.5$ although their conditional means differ. Whether, and in what sense, these two cells may be pooled is the question the next section answers.
:::

## The Propensity Score and Its Balancing Properties {#sec-w6-balancing}

The central insight of @rosenbaum1983central is that the $p$-dimensional adjustment problem of Chapter 5 reduces to a one-dimensional one. The right abstraction is the *balancing score*: any function of $X$ that renders treatment assignment conditionally independent of the covariates. The propensity score is the canonical --- and coarsest --- such function.

### Balancing Scores and the Propensity Score {#sec-w6-balancing-scores}

::: {#def-balancing-score}
## Balancing Score [@rosenbaum1983central]

A function $b(X)$ is called a **balancing score** if
$$T \indep X \mid b(X).$$
:::

The full covariate vector $X$ is trivially a balancing score: $T \indep X \mid X$ holds because, conditional on $X$, the conditional distribution of $X$ is degenerate and therefore cannot depend on treatment status. The propensity score is the *coarsest* balancing score (@lem-coarsest below), and therefore provides the greatest dimension reduction without sacrificing identification.

::: {#def-ps}
## Propensity Score [@rosenbaum1983central]

For a binary treatment $T \in \{0,1\}$ and observed covariates $X$, the **propensity score** is
$$\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X).$$
:::

In a randomized experiment, $\pi(X)$ is a known constant for all units --- equal to $0.5$ under balanced Bernoulli assignment ($P(T_i{=}1) = 0.5$ independently across units), and, marginally for each unit, under complete randomization with exactly $n/2$ treated, where the assignment indicators are dependent because the treated count is fixed. In an observational study, $\pi(X)$ varies with $X$ and must be estimated from data.

**Connection to strong ignorability.** Under strong ignorability $(Y(0),Y(1)) \indep T \mid X$, the potential outcomes carry no further information about treatment assignment once $X$ is given, so the treatment assignment mechanism satisfies
$$P\bigl(T{=}1 \mid X,\, Y(0),\, Y(1)\bigr) = P(T{=}1 \mid X) = \pi(X).$$
This equality is a *consequence* of the ignorability assumption, not part of the definition of $\pi(X)$. What unconfoundedness rules out is precisely any residual dependence of treatment on the potential outcomes after conditioning on $X$.

::: {#thm-balance}
## The Propensity Score Is a Balancing Score [@rosenbaum1983central]

$T \indep X \mid \pi(X)$.
:::

*Proof.* It suffices to show $P(T{=}1 \mid X, \pi(X)) = P(T{=}1 \mid \pi(X))$. Since $\pi(X)$ is a deterministic function of $X$, conditioning on both $X$ and $\pi(X)$ is the same as conditioning on $X$ alone, so $P(T{=}1 \mid X, \pi(X)) = P(T{=}1 \mid X) = \pi(X)$. For the right-hand side, the law of iterated expectations gives
$$P\bigl(T{=}1 \mid \pi(X)\bigr) = \E\bigl[P(T{=}1 \mid X) \,\big|\, \pi(X)\bigr] = \E\bigl[\pi(X) \,\big|\, \pi(X)\bigr] = \pi(X),$$
where the last equality holds because $\pi(X)$ is measurable with respect to itself. Hence both sides equal $\pi(X)$ and the conditional independence follows. $\square$

In the running example, the two cells with $\pi = 0.5$ together contain $200$ treated and $200$ control units, and within this pooled stratum the covariate $X$ is distributed identically in the two arms: half of the treated units and half of the controls come from each cell. That is the balancing property at work. It says nothing about outcomes: the two cells have different $\mu(t,x)$, and pooling them is harmless for estimating a causal effect only because of the theorem of the next subsection.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Covariate Balance and Design-Stage Analysis

@thm-balance has a practical consequence that @rubin2008objective and @imbens2015causal call *design before analysis*: covariate balance can be assessed before the outcome data are consulted. The balancing property implies
$$f\bigl(X \mid T{=}1,\, \pi(X)\bigr) = f\bigl(X \mid T{=}0,\, \pi(X)\bigr) \quad \text{a.s. on } \{0 < \pi(X) < 1\},$$
i.e., at every score value where both arms occur with positive probability, the conditional distribution of $X$ given the propensity score is the same in the two arms. Stratifying on a discretized $\hat\pi(X)$ and comparing covariate distributions within strata --- via standardized mean differences (defined in @sec-w6-balance-diagnostics), which are preferred over $t$-tests because they do not conflate imbalance with sample size --- diagnoses whether the propensity score model achieves adequate balance, without ever looking at $Y$. Because the diagnostic does not involve the outcome, specifications cannot be selected on the basis of favorable effect estimates. Analysts can --- and generally should --- iterate the propensity model in response to observed imbalance; doing so while blinded to $Y$ is what keeps the design stage objective. (@sec-w6-design-workflow develops the full design workflow, including the precise scope and limits of this outcome-blind iteration.)
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Observed Covariates Only

@thm-balance is a statement about the *observed* covariate distribution. It says that within strata of $\pi(X)$, the distribution of $X$ is the same in the treated and control groups. It does *not* say anything about unobserved confounders $U$: if $U$ affects both $T$ and $Y$ and is not captured by $X$, the balancing property fails to close the back-door path through $U$.
:::

### The Propensity Score Theorem {#sec-w6-ps-theorem}

The balancing property has a fundamental identification consequence: unconfoundedness at $X$ implies unconfoundedness at *any* balancing score of $X$, and in particular at the scalar $\pi(X)$. Before stating that result we record a structural fact about balancing scores: among all of them, the propensity score is the coarsest. The identification theorem can then be proved at full generality, with the propensity score case obtained by taking $b(X) = \pi(X)$.

::: {#lem-coarsest}
## The Propensity Score Is the Coarsest Balancing Score [@rosenbaum1983central]

If $b(X)$ is any balancing score --- that is, $T \indep X \mid b(X)$ --- then $\pi(X)$ is a function of $b(X)$: $\pi(X) = g(b(X))$ for some measurable function $g$.
:::

*Proof.* Since $b(X)$ is a balancing score, $T \indep X \mid b(X)$, which means $P(T{=}1 \mid X,\, b(X)) = P(T{=}1 \mid b(X))$. But $b(X)$ is a function of $X$, so conditioning on $b(X)$ is already implicit in conditioning on $X$:
$$\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X) = P\bigl(T{=}1 \mid X,\, b(X)\bigr) = P\bigl(T{=}1 \mid b(X)\bigr).$$
Hence $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid b(X))$, which is a measurable function of $b(X)$ alone. $\square$

The lemma is the precise statement of the *Rosenbaum--Rubin coarsest-balancing-score property*: the propensity score is a measurable function of every balancing score, $\pi(X) = g(b(X))$, or equivalently $\sigma\{\pi(X)\} \subseteq \sigma\{b(X)\}$. Every balancing score is therefore at least as fine as $\pi(X)$, which is what makes $\pi(X)$ the coarsest balancing score and the maximally parsimonious adjustment variable. The reverse factorization need *not* hold: a general balancing score --- $X$ itself, for example --- need not be a function of $\pi(X)$. (By analogy with classical sufficiency, $\pi(X)$ plays the role of a minimal sufficient reduction of $X$ for the treatment indicator, although no parametric model is involved here.) With the lemma in hand, the identification theorem is straightforward.

::: {#thm-ps}
## Propensity Score Theorem [@rosenbaum1983central]

Suppose joint conditional exchangeability holds: $(Y(0), Y(1)) \indep T \mid X$. Then for any balancing score $b(X)$,
$$\bigl(Y(0),\, Y(1)\bigr) \;\indep\; T \;\Big|\; b(X);$$
no positivity is needed for this conditional-independence transfer. If, in addition, $0 < \pi(X) < 1$ almost surely, then $0 < P(T{=}1 \mid b(X)) < 1$ almost surely as well, so *strong* ignorability given $X$ implies strong ignorability given $b(X)$, and adjustment for $b(X)$ identifies the potential-outcome means. In particular, taking $b(X) = \pi(X)$ gives strong ignorability with the scalar propensity score in place of the full covariate vector.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

Write $\mathbf{Y} = (Y(0), Y(1))$ for the pair of potential outcomes, and let $b(X)$ be any balancing score. By @lem-coarsest there is a measurable function $g$ with $\pi(X) = g(b(X))$. Since $b(X)$ is a function of $X$, the law of iterated expectations gives
$$\begin{aligned}
P\bigl(T{=}1 \mid \mathbf{Y},\, b(X)\bigr)
&= \E\bigl[P(T{=}1 \mid \mathbf{Y}, X) \mid \mathbf{Y}, b(X)\bigr] \\
&= \E\bigl[P(T{=}1 \mid X) \mid \mathbf{Y}, b(X)\bigr] \quad\text{(joint ignorability: } T \indep \mathbf{Y} \mid X\text{)} \\
&= \E\bigl[g\bigl(b(X)\bigr) \mid \mathbf{Y}, b(X)\bigr] = g\bigl(b(X)\bigr).
\end{aligned}$$
The same computation without $\mathbf{Y}$ in the conditioning set yields $P(T{=}1 \mid b(X)) = \E[\pi(X) \mid b(X)] = g(b(X))$. Hence $P(T{=}1 \mid \mathbf{Y}, b(X)) = P(T{=}1 \mid b(X))$, and because $T$ is binary, $\mathbf{Y} \indep T \mid b(X)$; note that positivity was not used in this argument. If additionally $0 < \pi(X) < 1$ almost surely, positivity transfers to the balancing score: $P(T{=}1 \mid b(X)) = \pi(X) \in (0,1)$ almost surely. Taking $b(X) = \pi(X)$, with $g$ the identity, gives the propensity score case. $\square$
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Two Misreadings of Identification via the Score

Combining @thm-ps with consistency and positivity yields an alternative identification formula. Define the arm-specific conditional mean functions
$$m_t(p) = \E\bigl[Y \mid T{=}t,\, \pi(X) = p\bigr], \qquad t \in \{0, 1\};$$
then
$$\E[Y(t)] = \E\bigl[m_t\bigl(\pi(X)\bigr)\bigr], \qquad m_1(p) - m_0(p) = \E\bigl[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid \pi(X) = p\bigr].$$
Two misreadings of this formula are common.

*Misreading 1: $m_t(\pi(x)) = \mu(t,x)$.* The two conditional regressions $\E[Y \mid \pi(X), T{=}t]$ and $\E[Y \mid X, T{=}t]$ are different functions and their pointwise values generally differ. By iterated expectations and the theorem, $m_t(p) = \E\{\mu(t,X) \mid \pi(X) = p\}$: the average of $\mu(t,\cdot)$ over the covariate values that share a score. In the running example, $m_1(0.5) = 8$ while $\mu(1,(1,0)) = 9$ and $\mu(1,(0,1)) = 7$; the effect conditional on the score, $m_1(0.5) - m_0(0.5) = 2$, is the average of the cell effects $3$ and $1$. Effects conditional on the score are identified; $\tau(x)$ for each covariate value is not recovered from the score alone. Only the marginal expectations agree:
$$\E\bigl[\E[Y \mid \pi(X),\, T{=}t]\bigr] = \E\bigl[\E[Y \mid X,\, T{=}t]\bigr] = \E[Y(t)].$$

*Misreading 2: regress $Y$ on $T$ and $\pi(X)$.* The formula licenses no particular parametric specification: identification through the propensity score requires that the arm-specific functions $m_t$ be estimated sufficiently well --- nonparametrically or by a correctly specified model --- and then standardized over the marginal distribution of $\pi(X)$. An arbitrary parametric regression of $Y$ on $T$ and $\pi(X)$ need not identify the ATE. Population least squares of $Y$ on $(1, T, \pi(X))$, for instance, gives the coefficient
$$\beta_T = \frac{\E\bigl[\pi(X)\{1-\pi(X)\}\{m_1(\pi(X)) - m_0(\pi(X))\}\bigr]}{\E\bigl[\pi(X)\{1-\pi(X)\}\bigr]},$$
a variance-weighted average of the score-conditional effects rather than the ATE. (By the Frisch--Waugh theorem, the residual of $T$ after projection on $(1,\pi(X))$ is $T - \pi(X)$, so $\beta_T = \E[\{T-\pi(X)\}Y]/\E[\{T-\pi(X)\}^2]$, and conditioning on $\pi(X)$ gives the display.) In the running example, $\pi(1-\pi)$ takes the values $0.16$, $0.25$, $0.16$ at the three score values, so $\beta_T = 0.456/0.196 = 114/49 \approx 2.33$, not $2.4$: the regression overweights the middle score, where $\pi(1-\pi)$ is largest.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Dimension Reduction

@thm-ps says that instead of adjusting for the full high-dimensional vector $X$, it is sufficient to adjust for the scalar $\pi(X)$. This reduces the *curse of dimensionality* in covariate adjustment from a $\dim(X)$-dimensional problem to a one-dimensional one. Together with consistency and positivity, identification of the ATE follows:
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E\bigl[\E[Y \mid T{=}1, \pi(X)] - \E[Y \mid T{=}0, \pi(X)]\bigr].$$
The score reduces dimension for adjustment; it is not a covariate to plug into an arbitrary model.
:::

### Subclassification on the Propensity Score {#sec-w6-subclassification}

The first estimator that the dimension reduction suggests is the stratified estimator of Chapter 5 with strata defined by the scalar $\hat\pi(X)$ instead of by cells of $X$. The score is a nuisance parameter, as the regression coefficient was in Chapter 5: fit $\hat\pi(X_i)$, then stratify on it. Choose boundaries $0 = b_0 < b_1 < \cdots < b_J = 1$ --- quantiles of $\hat\pi$ are the common choice --- and let $B_i(j) = \mathbb{I}\{b_{j-1} < \hat\pi(X_i) \le b_j\}$ indicate membership of unit $i$ in stratum $j$. Within stratum $j$ compare arm means, then average the stratum contrasts with the stratum shares:
$$\hat\tau(j) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n B_i(j)\,T_iY_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n B_i(j)\,T_i} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n B_i(j)(1-T_i)Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n B_i(j)(1-T_i)}, \qquad \hat\tau_{\mathrm{st}} = \sum_{j=1}^J \frac{n_j}{n}\,\hat\tau(j), \quad n_j = \sum_{i=1}^n B_i(j).$$ {#eq-w6-strat}
The weights $n_j/n$ target the ATE. Weighting the stratum contrasts by the treated shares instead,
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATT,st}} = \sum_{j=1}^J \frac{n_{1j}}{n_1}\,\hat\tau(j), \qquad n_{1j} = \sum_i B_i(j)T_i,\quad n_1 = \sum_i T_i,$$
targets the ATT. In the running example, taking the three score values as strata, the population version of @eq-w6-strat is $0.4 \times 2 + 0.4 \times 2 + 0.2 \times 4 = 2.4 = \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$, and the ATT version gives $(80 \times 2 + 200 \times 2 + 160 \times 4)/440 = 30/11 = \tau_{\mathrm{ATT}}$; the pooled stratum $\pi = 0.5$ contributes its score-conditional effect $2$, not either cell effect.

**What it costs.** With a continuous $X$, the score is only approximately constant within a stratum, so some confounding remains even when $\hat\pi$ is correct; more strata reduce it at the price of sparser cells and more variable $\hat\tau(j)$. With $J$ fixed, the residual bias does not vanish as $n$ grows --- a limitation of fixed-stratum subclassification, not of @thm-ps. For a single continuous confounder, under particular distributional models, @cochran1968effectiveness found that $J = 5$ strata of equal size remove about $90\%$ of the bias of the unadjusted comparison, and extending his normal-model calculation to $J = 10$ gives about $96\%$; quintiles of $\hat\pi$ are the common default. If either arm of a stratum is empty, $\hat\tau(j)$ is undefined: revise the grouping or the estimator, and if units or strata are dropped, state the resulting target population, since the full-population ATE is no longer automatically the target.

**Balance within strata is approximate.** The true score satisfies $T \indep X \mid \pi(X)$, but in practice one groups *estimated* scores into intervals $B(X)$, and two things can leave imbalance within a stratum: estimation error in $\hat\pi$, and variation of $\pi$ inside the interval, since $P\{T{=}1 \mid B(X)\} = \E\{\pi(X) \mid B(X)\} \ne \pi(X)$ unless $\pi$ is constant on the interval. Within-stratum balance, $\bar X_{1j} \approx \bar X_{0j}$ for every stratum $j$, is therefore something to *assess* with the diagnostics of @sec-w6-balance-diagnostics, not a theorem to invoke. Subclassification approximates adjustment on the score more and more closely as the strata become finer, provided both arms remain populated; matching (@sec-w6-matching) compares units with nearby scores by a separate rule, possibly reusing controls, and its matched sets need not partition the sample, so it is not the limit of the stratification estimator.

::: {#exm-pooling}
## Pooling Cells That Do Not Share a Score

Change one entry of the running example: let cell $(0,1)$ have $N_{1x} = 150$ treated units instead of $100$, so that $\pi(0,1) = 0.75 \ne 0.5$. The cells $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ no longer share a score value and the theorem no longer licenses pooling them. Pooling them anyway gives treated shares $(100,150)/250 = (0.4, 0.6)$ and control shares $(100,50)/150 = (0.67, 0.33)$ from the two cells: the pooled stratum is not balanced. Its pooled contrast is $(100 \times 9 + 150 \times 7)/250 - 6 = 1.8$, while the average effect in the two cells is $(3+1)/2 = 2$, and the resulting ATE calculation becomes $2.32$ instead of $2.4$. (The ATT calculation happens to survive here, at $125/49$, because both cells have control mean $6$: imbalance and bias for a given estimand are distinct claims.)
:::

## Constructing the Propensity Score {#sec-w6-constructing}

The true propensity score $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$ is *unknown* in observational studies and must be estimated from the data. Its practical construction, however, requires more than choosing a binary-response algorithm. Three logically distinct decisions must be kept separate. First, *causal reasoning* determines the pretreatment adjustment set $X$: the set must be sufficient to support conditional exchangeability, for example by blocking every back-door path from $T$ to $Y$ (Chapters 3 and 5). Second, *statistical modeling* determines how the treatment probability depends on the chosen covariates --- via logistic regression, nonlinear terms, interactions, regularization, or flexible machine-learning methods. Third, *design diagnostics* determine whether the fitted score actually produces adequate balance and overlap for the chosen estimand. A good predictive model for treatment does not automatically produce a good causal design, and no statistical treatment model can repair an invalid adjustment set chosen from an incorrect causal graph.

### Covariate Selection: What Belongs in $X$? {#sec-w6-covariate-selection}

The propensity score inherits its causal validity from the adjustment set on which it is conditioned. The primary rule is therefore graphical and scientific rather than predictive: $X$ should be a pretreatment set sufficient to block all back-door paths from $T$ to $Y$. The causal assumption is $Y(t) \indep T \mid X$; estimating $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$ cannot make this assumption true if it was false for the chosen $X$.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## What the Propensity Score Cannot Do

The propensity score balances the covariates included in $X$. It does not balance unmeasured confounders, repair adjustment for a collider, or justify conditioning on a post-treatment variable. The causal validity of $X$ must be established --- from subject-matter knowledge and the causal graph --- *before* the propensity score is estimated.
:::

**A bias--variance trade-off.** Among the pretreatment variables that keep the adjustment set valid, the choice of what to put in the score model trades bias against variance. *Too few covariates*: omitting a confounder, or a term the score model needs (a square, an interaction), misspecifies the score for adjustment, and the resulting bias does not shrink as $n$ grows. *Too many covariates*: a variable that is not needed for ignorability leaves a valid set valid, but it pushes the estimated scores toward zero or one, enlarges the weights, lowers the effective sample size (@sec-w6-balance-diagnostics), and adds estimation noise. The two costs are not symmetric. The variance cost of an unnecessary covariate falls as $n$ grows and is measured by the weight diagnostics. The bias of an omitted confounder does not fall with $n$, and no outcome-blind diagnostic can size it: a balance check on the omitted variable shows that the arms differ on it, not whether that difference matters for $Y$. When it is uncertain whether a pretreatment variable is a confounder, including it is therefore cheap insurance. The same reasoning applies to the functional form: richer terms in the score model cost variance and protect against misspecification bias, the lesson of Part 2 of the lab (@sec-w6-lab-part2). The insurance argument has two limits, taken up below: it covers only variables that keep the set valid, so mediators and colliders are excluded however uncertain one is; and a variable known to affect treatment only buys no protection and can amplify bias from unmeasured confounding.

::: {#exm-covsel}
## Insurance against an Omitted Confounder

Let $X_1, X_2$ be independent $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$, $T \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\{\expit(-0.3 + 0.6X_1 + 1.2X_2)\}$, and $Y = T + X_1 + \gamma X_2 + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathrm{N}(0,1)$, so that $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = 1$. The variable $X_2$ strongly predicts treatment. With $\gamma = 0$ it is unnecessary for adjustment; with $\gamma = 0.3$ it is a weak confounder. Fit the logistic score by maximum likelihood on $X_1$ alone or on $(X_1, X_2)$ and compute the Hájek ATE estimator; over $2{,}000$ replications at $n = 1{,}000$ (script `covsel19.R`, seed 19):

| **Score model on** | **Bias** ($\gamma = 0$) | **SD** ($\gamma = 0$) | **Bias** ($\gamma = 0.3$) | **SD** ($\gamma = 0.3$) |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $X_1$ only | $-0.002$ | $0.066$ | $0.281$ | $0.070$ |
| $X_1$ and $X_2$ | $0.000$ | $0.098$ | $0.000$ | $0.108$ |

With $\gamma = 0$, including $X_2$ costs variance: the SD rises from $0.066$ to $0.098$, and the control-arm effective sample size falls from about $95\%$ to $66\%$ of $n_0$. With $\gamma = 0.3$, omitting $X_2$ costs a bias of $0.281$, four times the SD, and the RMSE rises from $0.108$ to $0.289$. Here a wrong exclusion is far more expensive than a wrong inclusion, and only the cost of the inclusion is measured by the diagnostics.
:::

Where each variable sits on this trade-off depends on its role. Within a causally valid pretreatment set, candidate variables need not play identical roles. A useful first taxonomy classifies them by whether they predict treatment, outcome, both, or neither [@brookhart2006variable; @vanderweele2019principles]. The roles themselves come from the causal graph; the two "predicts" columns describe tendencies, not definitions. In particular, a treatment predictor can predict the *observed* outcome through $T$ without predicting the potential outcomes given a valid adjustment set, so predictive association with $Y$ does not by itself make a variable a confounder.

| **Variable type** | **Predicts $T$?** | **Predicts $Y$?** | **Typical recommendation** |
|---|:---:|:---:|---|
| Confounder | yes | yes | include |
| Outcome predictor only | no or weakly | yes | usually include (balance it) |
| Treatment predictor only | yes | no | include only with caution |
| Predictor of neither | no | no | usually unnecessary |

Variables related to both treatment and outcome are central confounders and should ordinarily be included: they are needed to block back-door paths. Pretreatment variables that strongly predict the outcome may be useful even when they predict treatment only weakly, because they can improve precision; residual imbalance in a strong outcome predictor can matter greatly, so balance on such variables deserves priority in the diagnostics. Variables that strongly predict treatment but are unrelated to the potential outcomes require more caution: although they improve prediction of $T$, they can push estimated scores toward zero or one, reduce overlap and effective sample size, and inflate the variance of weighted estimators without removing appreciable confounding bias; moreover, conditioning on such a near-instrument can *amplify* the bias arising from any residual unmeasured confounding. Pure noise variables mainly add estimation variability and may worsen finite-sample balance, especially with flexible learners.

These are tendencies rather than universal rules, and they do not justify automatic variable deletion. Whether a variable is truly unrelated to the potential outcomes is a scientific judgment subject to uncertainty, and plausible pretreatment confounders should generally be retained even when their treatment-model coefficients are small or statistically insignificant.

The adjustment set is validated as a whole, not variable by variable. For ordinary propensity-score adjustment aimed at a total effect, use a pretreatment set that blocks every back-door path, and do not adjust for mediators or for variables that open otherwise blocked noncausal paths. *Post-treatment variables* --- variables affected by treatment --- should not be conditioned on: doing so can block part of the causal effect, induce selection bias, and change the estimand. *Pretreatment colliders* can be equally damaging despite being measured before treatment: in the M-structure of panel (b) below, the variable $C$ is pretreatment, yet conditioning on it opens the noncausal path $T \leftarrow U_1 \rightarrow C \leftarrow U_2 \rightarrow Y$ that is blocked when $C$ is left alone (Chapter 3). Whether a node acts as a collider is path-specific, and whether a set is a valid adjustment set depends on the whole graph and on the rest of the set; the conclusions drawn from the three panels are conclusions for those graphs. "Include every available variable" is in any case not a safe default.

### Parametric Estimation by Logistic Regression {#sec-w6-logistic}

The classical approach models
$$\log\frac{\pi(X)}{1 - \pi(X)} = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j X_j + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \gamma_j\, h_j(X_j) + \sum_{j<k} \delta_{jk}\, X_j X_k,$$
where the $h_j$ are optional nonlinear transformations (polynomials, splines) and the cross-product terms capture interactions among covariates, and estimates the coefficients by maximum likelihood. The fitted values $\hat\pi(X_i)$ are used in place of the true propensity score. Linearity on the logit scale in the raw covariates is an assumption, not a default truth: nonlinear terms and covariate-by-covariate interactions are often needed to achieve balance. (Treatment-by-covariate interactions have no place in this model --- treatment is the *response* here.) Terms should be added based on causal knowledge and the balance diagnostics of @sec-w6-balance-diagnostics, not predictive fit alone.

Variable selection by treatment-model $p$-values is generally inappropriate. A covariate may be an important confounder or outcome predictor even when its coefficient in the treatment model is small or statistically insignificant, and removing it can worsen causal balance without materially changing treatment-prediction accuracy. Backward selection driven by significance serves sparse prediction, which is not the objective of a propensity model. (Maximum likelihood is not the only way to fit the logistic model; @sec-w6-calibration fits the same model so that the inverse-probability weights balance the covariates exactly.)

### Flexible and Machine-Learning Estimators {#sec-w6-ml}

When $X$ is high-dimensional or when the true propensity score is non-linear, machine learning methods --- gradient boosted trees, random forests, regularized logistic regression (LASSO, ridge) --- can estimate $\pi(X)$ more flexibly, reducing misspecification of the treatment model without fully prespecifying nonlinearities and interactions. Predictive accuracy alone, however, is not the relevant success criterion: hyperparameters tuned solely to classification loss (log loss, AUC) may improve prediction precisely by producing more extreme probability estimates, which destabilizes the resulting weights. A related issue is *overfitting*: an estimator that (nearly) perfectly separates treated and control units in-sample produces fitted scores near one for treated units and near zero for controls, mimicking an overlap violation that need not exist in the population. Cross-fitting (Chapter 12) removes the *same-sample* component of this problem by evaluating each unit's score on a fold not used to fit it, but it does not create overlap and does not prevent extreme out-of-fold predictions: a genuinely near-deterministic treatment rule yields extreme scores on held-out data as well. Regularization, overlap diagnostics, and --- when scientifically justified --- trimming or re-targeting the estimand (developed later in this chapter) remain separate requirements. Whatever the learner, the fitted design must ultimately be evaluated through the balance and overlap it delivers; no machine-learning method eliminates the need for causal covariate selection or design diagnostics.

### The Goal Is Balance, Not Treatment Prediction {#sec-w6-balance-not-prediction}

A well-specified propensity model is still a model for $P(T{=}1 \mid X)$, and accurate prediction is not itself a defect. It is, however, insufficient as a criterion. In ordinary classification, a model is rewarded for separating the two classes. In propensity-score analysis, strong separation signals trouble: fitted scores near one for treated units and near zero for controls mean little common support, extreme inverse-probability weights $1/\hat\pi(X_i)$ and $1/\{1-\hat\pi(X_i)\}$, and an estimator whose value depends on a handful of observations. A high AUC may therefore indicate a difficult causal comparison rather than a successful design. Note also that the AUC depends only on the *ranking* of the fitted probabilities --- it is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of them --- so it says nothing about how extreme the probabilities, and hence the weights, are. High AUC does not establish covariate balance, overlap, or causal validity; an additional treatment predictor can improve discrimination without improving confounding control. Treatment probabilities, balance, and weight stability must be evaluated separately, and a needed confounder is never dropped to make the arms look more alike.

The estimated score, moreover, is a design device, not the final diagnostic object. Conditioning on the *true* score balances $X$ in distribution (@thm-balance), but matching or weighting approximately on an *estimated* score does not guarantee adequate finite-sample balance. After matching or weighting, balance must therefore be assessed on the original covariates and, when scientifically relevant, on nonlinear functions and interactions of them; similar distributions of $\hat\pi(X)$ across arms do not by themselves establish that the underlying covariates are balanced.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Propensity Score Estimation Is a Nuisance, Not the Goal

The propensity score is estimated in order to construct a good estimator of $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$. Balance diagnostics --- checking whether $\E[X \mid T{=}1, \hat\pi(X) \approx p] \approx \E[X \mid T{=}0, \hat\pi(X) \approx p]$ --- assess whether the estimated score has achieved covariate balance on the *observed* covariates, but they say nothing about whether unobserved confounders are balanced. Relatedly, high treatment-prediction accuracy is not the goal: the estimated score is judged by the balance and overlap it delivers for the causal target, not by its classification performance.
:::

### Balance and Overlap Diagnostics {#sec-w6-balance-diagnostics}

The standard scalar diagnostic for covariate balance is the *standardized mean difference* (SMD). For covariate $X_j$, let $\bar X_{1j}$ and $\bar X_{0j}$ denote the treated and control sample means and $s_{1j}^2$ and $s_{0j}^2$ the corresponding sample variances. Then
$$\mathrm{SMD}(X_j) = \frac{\bar X_{1j} - \bar X_{0j}}{\sqrt{\bigl(s_{1j}^2 + s_{0j}^2\bigr)/2}};$$
for a binary covariate, the numerator is the difference in proportions, with the analogous pooled scale in the denominator. Dividing by the pooled scale makes the diagnostic free of the units of $X_j$ and --- unlike a $t$-statistic --- insensitive to the sample size, so it measures the magnitude of imbalance rather than its statistical detectability. A common informal benchmark treats $|\mathrm{SMD}| \le 0.1$ as adequate balance; this is a heuristic, not a test, and whether residual imbalance is consequential depends on how strongly the covariate predicts the outcome, on the sample size, and on the estimand. An SMD below the benchmark means the means are *approximately* balanced, not equal. For weighted or matched analyses, the arm means are replaced by their design-weighted counterparts (with weights given by the scheme in use, and reused control units counted with their matching multiplicities); the denominator, however, should be held fixed at the pre-adjustment pooled scale, so that before-and-after values are directly comparable.

Balance of means alone can be inadequate when the outcome depends nonlinearly on the covariates. Useful supplements include variance ratios, quantile differences, empirical-distribution plots, and SMDs computed on squares, interactions, and other scientifically relevant transformations of the covariates.

Balance and overlap are distinct, and both must be checked: a design can show good mean balance after weighting while relying on a few extreme weights, and raw overlap can look reasonable while nonlinear imbalance remains. Overlap diagnostics start with plots of the estimated score distributions in the two arms on a common scale. Which comparison matters depends on the estimand: for the ATT, the question is whether the control scores cover the treated-score distribution; for the ATE, both arms must cover the full target population. Weight summaries --- minimum, maximum, selected quantiles, and the coefficient of variation --- expose instability directly. For matching, the bookkeeping of the design plays the same role: the number of unmatched treated units, the number of distinct controls used and how often each is reused, and the distribution of match distances.

The cost of extreme weights can be summarized by the *effective sample size* of a weighted arm with nonnegative weights $\{w_i\}$,
$$n_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\bigl(\sum_i w_i\bigr)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2},$$
which equals the actual sample size when the weights are constant and collapses toward $1$ when a single weight dominates. For two-arm estimators it is usually most informative arm by arm: $n_{\mathrm{eff},t} = \bigl(\sum_{i: T_i = t} w_i\bigr)^2 / \sum_{i: T_i = t} w_i^2$. Its interpretation as a sample size is exact under a simple model: for independent outcomes with common variance $\sigma^2$ and weights treated as fixed, $\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\sum_i w_iY_i/\sum_i w_i \mid w\bigr) = \sigma^2/n_{\mathrm{eff}}$, so a weighted arm with $500$ units but $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = 40$ behaves like $40$ equally weighted observations. Heterogeneous variances, varying conditional means, estimated weights, and reused controls all complicate this reading; in general $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ summarizes the concentration of the weights and is a diagnostic rather than the estimator's actual precision. Reporting it alongside the point estimate makes the price of near-overlap violations concrete.

### Design Objectives Depend on the Estimand {#sec-w6-design-objectives}

The same propensity model need not serve every estimator equally, so the diagnostics above should be tailored to the target. For *matching* (developed in @sec-w6-matching), the score must support close matches and covariate balance within the matched sample; the relevant diagnostics are match distances, residual SMDs among matched units, unmatched treated units, and control reuse. For *ATE weighting*, with weights $1/\hat\pi(X_i)$ for treated and $1/\{1-\hat\pi(X_i)\}$ for control units, both arms are re-weighted to the full target population, so weighted balance in both arms, weight tails, and arm-specific effective sample sizes are the primary concerns. For *ATT weighting*, with weights
$$w_i = T_i + (1 - T_i)\,\frac{\hat\pi(X_i)}{1 - \hat\pi(X_i)},$$
the treated arm is left unweighted and the central question is whether the controls can represent the treated units, so control coverage of the treated-score distribution is the key diagnostic. (These are the weights whose population versions appear in the third identity of @lem-weighted-balance and in the lab's HJ-ATT estimator.)

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Overlap Weights

The *overlap weights* $w_i = T_i\{1 - \hat\pi(X_i)\} + (1 - T_i)\,\hat\pi(X_i)$ emphasize units with scores near $1/2$ and are bounded by construction, so trimming is not needed merely to control divergent inverse weights; covariate balance, finite-sample support in both arms, and the causal validity of $X$ must still be assessed. Bounded weights do not guarantee adequate information: the target requires $\E[\pi(X)\{1-\pi(X)\}] > 0$, and when overlap is thin the effective information can still be small. The price is a change of estimand: they target the average effect in the overlap population, whose covariate density is proportional to $\pi(x)\{1-\pi(x)\}f_X(x)$ --- an instance of the re-targeting idea of @sec-w6-retargeting --- rather than the original ATE.
:::

The figure below displays the four weighting schemes as functions of the propensity score. The picture makes estimand targeting immediate: each scheme up-weights the units that must stand in for the population it targets, and instability appears exactly where a required weight diverges.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

The general principle: a propensity model cannot be evaluated independently of the estimand and the estimator that will use it.

### A Design-Stage Workflow {#sec-w6-design-workflow}

Propensity-score design is typically *iterative*: specify a treatment model, construct the proposed matched or weighted sample, assess balance and overlap, revise the design when the diagnostics are inadequate, and repeat. Revisions may include nonlinear terms, interactions, an alternative link or learner, regularization, a modified matching ratio or caliper, a different weighting target, or trimming. The outcome data remain hidden throughout this cycle.

Outcome blinding, in particular, does not mean that the specification is fixed after one fit. Three levels should be distinguished. *Outcome-blind design*: no outcome data are used to choose the treatment model or the design --- not merely that no effect estimate is inspected; prior scientific knowledge about which covariates predict the outcome is compatible with this principle and should inform the adjustment set. *Balance-driven revision*: altering the model in response to observed imbalance is legitimate --- indeed expected. *Design lock*: once balance and overlap are judged acceptable, the matching or weighting rule is fixed, and only then are outcomes analyzed. The benefit is not that subjectivity disappears; it is that design decisions cannot be selected because they produce a preferred causal estimate.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A Propensity-Score Design Workflow

1. **Define the estimand.** Decide whether the target is the ATE, ATT, ATC, or an overlap-population effect.
2. **Specify the causal adjustment set.** Use subject-matter knowledge and the causal graph to select pretreatment variables that block all back-door paths. Exclude post-treatment variables and colliders.
3. **Specify an initial treatment model.** Include plausible nonlinear terms and interactions among covariates when needed. Do not select variables by treatment-model significance.
4. **Construct the design.** Apply the intended matching or weighting procedure.
5. **Assess covariate balance.** Examine standardized mean differences, distributional diagnostics, and balance of scientifically relevant transformations and interactions.
6. **Assess overlap and stability.** Inspect score distributions, match distances, weight tails, effective sample sizes, and the number of unmatched or trimmed units.
7. **Revise without using outcomes.** Modify the model or design until balance and overlap are acceptable, or conclude that the original target population is not supportable.
8. **Lock the design and analyze outcomes.** After the design is fixed, estimate the causal effect and quantify uncertainty validly for the chosen procedure.
:::

::: {#exm-auc}
## Variable Selection: Higher AUC, Worse Design

Consider five candidate variables for a treatment--outcome study: age $A$ and baseline severity $S$, each affecting both treatment and outcome; hospital preference $H$, strongly predictive of treatment but essentially unrelated to the potential outcomes; post-treatment adherence $M$; and a pretreatment collider $C$ driven by two latent variables as in panel (b) of the covariate-role figure. Compare three propensity models:
$$\text{Model 1: } \pi(A, S), \qquad \text{Model 2: } \pi(A, S, H), \qquad \text{Model 3: } \pi(A, S, H, M, C).$$
Model 1 contains the essential adjustment set. Model 2 predicts treatment better but, if $H$ nearly determines treatment, pushes fitted scores toward the boundaries, inflating weights and shrinking the effective sample size without removing additional confounding. Model 3 is causally invalid regardless of its fit: it conditions on the mediator $M$ and the collider $C$. Qualitatively, as an illustrative scenario rather than a general ordering:

| **Model** | **AUC** | **Max weight** | $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | **Causally valid?** |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| $\pi(A,S)$ | moderate | moderate | high | yes |
| $\pi(A,S,H)$ | high | large | low | yes, but imprecise |
| $\pi(A,S,H,M,C)$ | very high | extreme | poor | no |

The model with the highest AUC is the worst causal design, for two different reasons: $H$ makes it imprecise, $M$ and $C$ make it invalid.
:::

::: {#exm-reinisch}
## A Case Study of the Workflow: Prenatal Barbiturate Exposure

@imbens2015causal, Chapter 13, illustrate the design stage with the study of @reinisch1995utero on in utero exposure to barbiturates and adult cognitive outcomes: $7{,}943$ Copenhagen births, of which $745$ were exposed, with seventeen pretreatment covariates on the mother and the pregnancy. The exposed group differs systematically from the unexposed: higher socioeconomic status, older mothers, more pregnancy complications. The propensity model is built in three steps. (1) A *substantive set* --- the child's sex, the mother's age, socioeconomic status --- enters the logistic model regardless of its association with exposure. (2) *Linear terms* for the remaining covariates are proposed one at a time by their likelihood-ratio contribution to the treatment model, while that contribution exceeds a threshold. (3) *Second-order terms*, squares and interactions, are proposed by the same rule with a lower threshold. The sample is then subclassified on $\hat\pi$ and covariate balance is assessed within strata, as in @sec-w6-subclassification.

This procedure is consistent with the warning against selecting variables by treatment-model $p$-values, and it is worth seeing why. Step 1 fixes the confounders on causal grounds, and they are retained whatever their coefficients. Steps 2 and 3 *propose* additional terms by treatment-model fit; the design is then judged by the covariate balance it produces, not by the fit. Nothing substantive is dropped, and likelihood-ratio screening does not itself guarantee balance --- the balance assessment is a separate step that can send the analyst back to the model. The warning is against *dropping* a plausible confounder because its coefficient is small; it is not against adding terms until the strata are balanced, which is exactly the balance-driven revision of the workflow.
:::

## Matching on the Propensity Score {#sec-w6-matching}

The propensity score also motivates *matching*: for each treated unit $i$, find a control unit $j$ with $\hat\pi(X_j) \approx \hat\pi(X_i)$, and use $Y_j$ as a local estimate of $\E\bigl[Y(0) \mid \pi(X) = \pi(X_i)\bigr]$ [@abadie2006large; @abadie2016matching]. It is important to be precise about what is being estimated: the matched control outcome $Y_j$ is not a substitute for the individual counterfactual $Y_i(0)$, which is unobservable and contains an irreducible idiosyncratic component. Rather, $Y_j$ is a noisy local approximation to the *conditional mean* $\E[Y(0) \mid \pi(X) = \pi(X_i)]$, which is identified from observed control outcomes via the chain
$$\E[Y(0) \mid \pi(X) = \pi(X_i)] \;=\; \E[Y(0) \mid \pi(X) = \pi(X_i),\, T = 0] \;=\; \E[Y \mid \pi(X) = \pi(X_i),\, T = 0],$$
where the first equality uses @thm-ps ($Y(0) \indep T \mid \pi(X)$ under strong ignorability) and the second uses consistency ($Y = Y(0)$ when $T = 0$); positivity on the control side makes the conditional mean well defined. Averaging across treated units targets --- and, under the regularity conditions discussed below, consistently estimates --- the ATT:
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\, T_i=1} \Bigl[Y_i - Y_{\hat\jmath(i)}\Bigr],$$
where $n_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n T_i$ is the number of treated units and $\hat\jmath(i)$ is the index of the matched control unit. This is the third implementation of one identification formula: stratify (@sec-w6-subclassification), weight (@sec-w6-ipw), match.

### One-to-One Nearest Neighbor Matching {#sec-w6-nnm}

The most common matching algorithm is *nearest-neighbor* (1:1) matching [@abadie2006large]: for each treated unit $i$, find
$$\hat\jmath(i) = \arg\min_{j:\, T_j=0} \bigl|\hat\pi(X_i) - \hat\pi(X_j)\bigr|.$$
When several controls are equally close, a convention is required --- deterministic tie-breaking (e.g., the smallest index), averaging the outcomes of all equally close controls, or random selection; the choice affects the exact estimator and its variance, though not the identification logic.

Matched control units may be selected with or without replacement. With replacement, every treated unit receives its closest control, so matches are closer; the price is that a few controls may be reused many times, which reduces the effective amount of control information. Without replacement, each control is used once, the procedure needs at least as many available controls as retained treated units, and match quality degrades as the pool empties. Smaller match distances do not by themselves imply a universal ordering of bias or variance between the two schemes.

Matching with replacement is weighting with integer weights. If $K_j$ denotes the number of treated units matched to control $j$, then
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{NNM}} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\, T_i=1} Y_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j:\, T_j=0} K_j\, Y_j,$$ {#eq-w6-nnm-weights}
so the control arm is reweighted by $K_j/n_1$, a data-dependent analogue of the ATT odds weights of @sec-w6-design-objectives. The identity makes control reuse visible --- a control with large $K_j$ carries a large weight --- and is the starting point for the variance theory cited below.

### Caliper Matching {#sec-w6-caliper}

Caliper matching restricts matches to pairs within a maximum distance $\delta$ (the "caliper") on the propensity score scale:
$$\hat\jmath(i) = \arg\min_{j:\, T_j=0,\; |\hat\pi(X_i) - \hat\pi(X_j)| \le \delta} \bigl|\hat\pi(X_i) - \hat\pi(X_j)\bigr|.$$
Treated units with no control match within the caliper are discarded. The caliper may be defined on the probability scale, as written here, or --- commonly in practice --- on the logit scale $\mathrm{logit}\,\hat\pi(X)$, which spaces units more evenly near the boundaries of $[0,1]$; the chosen scale must be reported, since numerical caliper values are not comparable across scales. Because matchable treated units are retained and the rest discarded, the procedure no longer targets the original ATT: it targets an ATT restricted to the retained treated subpopulation with adequate overlap. Dropping treated units changes the finite-sample target, and the population version of that target depends on the limiting retention rule, the caliper, and the control support, not only on the convergence of $\hat\pi$; under adequate overlap a fixed caliper eventually retains nearly all treated units.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Matching as Nonparametric Regression on $\pi(X)$

The key idea behind propensity score matching is that it implicitly fits a *nonparametric regression* of $Y$ on $\pi(X)$ separately within each treatment arm. By @thm-ps, $(Y(0), Y(1)) \indep T \mid \pi(X)$, so the conditional mean $\E[Y(t) \mid \pi(X) = p]$ is identified from observed data for each $t \in \{0, 1\}$. Nearest-neighbor matching imputes the missing $Y_i(0)$ at each observed $\hat\pi(X_i)$ by the outcome of one close match: local constant regression on the propensity score with a single neighbor. A fixed-number imputation of this kind retains the outcome noise of the matched unit, so it is not pointwise consistent for the conditional mean; consistency of the *averaged* ATT estimator is a separate result that requires the regularity conditions stated in the warning below. The dimension reduction from @thm-ps is what makes the smoothing one-dimensional: instead of smoothing over the full covariate vector $X$, one smooths over the scalar $\pi(X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Design Transparency

Propensity score matching provides *design transparency*: by inspecting matched pairs, the analyst can directly assess whether treated and control units are similar on observed covariates. Comparing $\bar X_1$ and $\bar X_0$ within matched pairs via standardized mean differences is a standard pre-analysis diagnostic that can be conducted without consulting the outcome $Y$. In practice, the propensity specification should be revised until the matched sample shows satisfactory balance on the original covariates (@sec-w6-design-workflow), not merely small distances in the estimated score.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Inference after Matching Is Nonstandard

Matching estimators with a fixed number of matches are not classical sample averages. Reusing controls induces dependence among the matched contrasts, since the same control can serve several treated units; when matching directly on a multidimensional $X$, the estimator carries a bias term that can dominate the $\sqrt{n}$ rate [@abadie2006large]; and the ordinary bootstrap over units fails to reproduce the sampling distribution of a fixed-number-of-matches estimator [@abadie2008failure]. Valid standard errors require purpose-built variance estimators, and when the propensity score is estimated rather than known, the estimation error in $\hat\pi$ must additionally be accounted for [@abadie2016matching].

Consistency of the matching estimator itself also requires more than strong ignorability: sufficient accuracy (or balancing behavior) of the fitted score, smoothness of the relevant conditional mean functions, and match discrepancies that vanish asymptotically. The contrast with weighting should be stated precisely: for the smooth, regular weighting estimators of @sec-w6-ipw, resampling observations and refitting the score in each replication is valid under the conditions stated there; for fixed-number nearest-neighbor matching, the ordinary bootstrap is generally invalid and inference appropriate to the matching estimator must be used.
:::

### The Prognostic Score: The Outcome-Side Mirror {#sec-w6-prognostic}

The propensity score reduces $X$ to what bears on treatment. @hansen2008prognostic proposed the mirror image: reduce $X$ to what bears on the untreated outcome. The ignorability condition $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$ is symmetric in $T$ and $Y(0)$, and the theory of @sec-w6-balancing carries over with the two exchanged.

::: {#def-prognostic}
## Prognostic Score [@hansen2008prognostic]

A function $\Psi(X)$ is called a **prognostic score** if
$$Y(0) \indep X \mid \Psi(X).$$
:::

As with balancing scores, $X$ itself is trivially a prognostic score. Hansen's examples: under a location model $Y(0) = m_0(X) + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \indep X$, the scalar $m_0(X) = \E\{Y(0) \mid X\}$ is a prognostic score; under a generalized linear model for $Y(0)$ given $X$, so is the linear predictor; and when the variance of $Y(0)$ also depends on $X$, the mean and variance functions together form a two-dimensional prognostic score. The definition is stated for $Y(0)$ because $Y(0)$ is observed in the control arm, from which a prognostic score is estimated, and because $Y(0)$ is what the ATT must impute.

::: {#lem-prog-coarsest}
## The Conditional Law of $Y(0)$ Is the Coarsest Prognostic Score

Let $F_0(y \mid X) = P\{Y(0) \le y \mid X\}$. Then (i) $F_0(\cdot \mid X)$ is a prognostic score; and (ii) if $\Psi(X)$ is any prognostic score, $F_0(\cdot \mid X)$ is a function of $\Psi(X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

(i) Since $F_0(\cdot \mid X)$ is a function of $X$, $P\{Y(0) \le y \mid X, F_0(\cdot \mid X)\} = F_0(y \mid X)$, while $P\{Y(0) \le y \mid F_0(\cdot \mid X)\} = \E\{F_0(y \mid X) \mid F_0(\cdot \mid X)\} = F_0(y \mid X)$. The two conditional laws agree for every $y$, so $Y(0) \indep X \mid F_0(\cdot \mid X)$.

(ii) If $\Psi(X)$ is a prognostic score, then for every $y$, $F_0(y \mid X) = P\{Y(0) \le y \mid X, \Psi(X)\} = P\{Y(0) \le y \mid \Psi(X)\}$, a function of $\Psi(X)$.
:::

Part (i) is @thm-balance with $Y(0)$ in place of $T$, and part (ii) is @lem-coarsest: the mirror of $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$ is the whole conditional law of $Y(0)$. For a binary $T$ the conditional law is its mean, which is why the coarsest balancing score is a scalar; for a general $Y(0)$ the law needs more than its mean. Under the location model, $F_0(y \mid X) = P(\varepsilon \le y - m_0(X))$ is a function of $m_0(X)$, so $m_0(X)$ is the coarsest prognostic score. Without such a model $m_0(X)$ is in general not a prognostic score, but it still suffices for mean contrasts, as part (iii) of the next theorem shows.

::: {#thm-prognostic}
## Prognostic Score Theorem

Suppose $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$.

(i) For any prognostic score $\Psi(X)$, $Y(0) \indep T \mid \Psi(X)$.

(ii) If, in addition, consistency holds, $\E|Y(0)| < \infty$, and $P\{T{=}1 \mid \Psi(X)\} < 1$ almost surely, then
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = \E\Bigl[\E\{Y \mid T{=}1, \Psi(X)\} - \E\{Y \mid T{=}0, \Psi(X)\} \Bigm| T{=}1\Bigr].$$

(iii) The conclusion of (ii) holds with $\Psi(X)$ replaced by $m_0(X) = \E\{Y(0) \mid X\}$, provided $P\{T{=}1 \mid m_0(X)\} < 1$ almost surely, whether or not $m_0(X)$ is a prognostic score.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

(i) Let $A$ be any measurable set. Because $\Psi(X)$ is a function of $X$, iterated expectations conditioning on $(T, X)$ give
$$\begin{aligned} P\{Y(0) \in A \mid T, \Psi(X)\} &= \E\bigl[P\{Y(0) \in A \mid T, X\} \bigm| T, \Psi(X)\bigr] \\ &= \E\bigl[P\{Y(0) \in A \mid X\} \bigm| T, \Psi(X)\bigr] \quad\text{(ignorability)} \\ &= \E\bigl[P\{Y(0) \in A \mid \Psi(X)\} \bigm| T, \Psi(X)\bigr] \quad\text{(prognostic score)} \\ &= P\{Y(0) \in A \mid \Psi(X)\}. \end{aligned}$$
The conditional law of $Y(0)$ given $(T, \Psi(X))$ does not depend on $T$, which is the claim. These are the steps of the proof of @thm-ps with $T$ and $Y(0)$ exchanged.

(ii) By iterated expectations and consistency, $\E\{Y(1) \mid T{=}1\} = \E[\E\{Y \mid T{=}1, \Psi(X)\} \mid T{=}1]$. For the control mean,
$$\begin{aligned} \E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\} &= \E\bigl[\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1, \Psi(X)\} \bigm| T{=}1\bigr] = \E\bigl[\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}0, \Psi(X)\} \bigm| T{=}1\bigr] \\ &= \E\bigl[\E\{Y \mid T{=}0, \Psi(X)\} \bigm| T{=}1\bigr], \end{aligned}$$
by (i) in the middle step, which is well defined because $P\{T{=}0 \mid \Psi(X)\} > 0$, and consistency in the last.

(iii) The proof of (ii) used (i) only through $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1, \Psi\} = \E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}0, \Psi\}$. For $m_0(X)$ and $t \in \{0, 1\}$, $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}t, m_0(X)\} = \E[\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}t, X\} \mid T{=}t, m_0(X)] = \E\{m_0(X) \mid T{=}t, m_0(X)\} = m_0(X)$, using $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$ in the middle step, so the two conditional means agree.
:::

Parts (i) and (ii) are Propositions 3 and 4 of @hansen2008prognostic. Part (ii) is the ATT formula of @cor-ipw-att with $\Psi(X)$ in place of $X$, and part (iii) explains why the proof of that corollary could take $h = m_0(X)$: for a mean target, the location-model score is enough.

**Where the mirror breaks.** The first four rows of @tbl-mirror are exact mirror images; the last four are where the exchange of $T$ and $Y(0)$ fails, and each failure has one source: $T$ is binary and observed for every unit, while $Y(0)$ is general and observed only for controls. Positivity is the most consequential. For a balancing score, $P\{T{=}1 \mid b(X)\} = \pi(X)$ because $\pi$ is a function of $b$, so positivity in $b(X)$ and in $X$ are equivalent. For a prognostic score, $P\{T{=}1 \mid \Psi(X)\} = \E\{\pi(X) \mid \Psi(X)\}$ only averages $\pi$, so the overlap condition of part (ii) can hold although $\pi(x) = 1$ on part of the treated support, where the ATT is not identified by adjustment for $X$ (@sec-w6-retargeting). The gain is bought with outcome knowledge: at such $x$ no control is observed, so the value of $\Psi(x)$ comes from a model fitted to controls elsewhere and extrapolated. The model, not the data, supplies that part of the answer, as with any parametric extrapolation.

|  | **Balancing side** | **Prognostic side** |
|---|---|---|
| *The mirror: exchange $T$ and $Y(0)$* | | |
| Definition | $T \indep X \mid b(X)$ (@def-balancing-score) | $Y(0) \indep X \mid \Psi(X)$ (@def-prognostic) |
| Canonical score | $\pi(X) = P(T{=}1 \mid X)$ (@thm-balance) | $F_0(\cdot \mid X) = P\{Y(0) \le \cdot \mid X\}$ (@lem-prog-coarsest) |
| Coarsest | $\pi$ is a function of every $b$ (@lem-coarsest) | $F_0(\cdot \mid X)$ is a function of every $\Psi$ (@lem-prog-coarsest) |
| Ignorability transfers | $(Y(0), Y(1)) \indep T \mid b(X)$ (@thm-ps) | $Y(0) \indep T \mid \Psi(X)$ (@thm-prognostic) |
| *Where the mirror breaks* | | |
| Size of the score | a scalar: the law of a binary $T$ is its mean | a distribution; $m_0(X)$ under a location model, and $m_0$ suffices for means |
| Positivity transfers | both ways: $P\{T{=}1 \mid b(X)\} = \pi(X)$ | one way: $P\{T{=}1 \mid \Psi(X)\} = \E\{\pi(X) \mid \Psi(X)\}$; $\Psi$ is extrapolated where $\pi = 1$ |
| Outcomes covered | both: ATE, ATT, and ATC from one score | $Y(0)$ only: the ATT; the ATE needs a score for $Y(1)$ too |
| Fitting and checks | all units, outcome-blind | controls only, using outcomes |

: @sec-w6-balancing and its mirror: balancing scores [@rosenbaum1983central] and prognostic scores [@hansen2008prognostic]. {#tbl-mirror}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Estimating and Using a Prognostic Score

A prognostic score is unknown and must be fitted, and only the controls carry information about it. @hansen2008prognostic documents two consequences. Fitting the score on the same controls that are then used for adjustment overfits: in his simulation with well-separated arms, a nominal $0.05$ test of no effect rejected about $18\%$ of the time, and fitting on a separate sample of controls, such as historical controls, removed the problem. Fitting on both arms instead mixes prognosis with propensity and can bias the comparison. The use of control outcomes also sits uneasily with the outcome-blind design of @sec-w6-design-workflow: a score fitted on the study's own controls brings outcome data into the design stage, and a separate control sample is what keeps the design outcome-blind.

For the ATE, the score must also be sufficient for $Y(1)$, which fails when a covariate modifies the effect; Hansen's Proposition 5 adds the effect modifier to the conditioning set. Finally, the two scores combine well. If $\Psi(X)$ is a prognostic score, so is $(\pi(X), \Psi(X))$, since adding a function of $X$ preserves $Y(0) \indep X \mid \Psi(X)$; and if $\pi$ is correct, $(\pi(X), \Psi(X))$ is a balancing score, since $\pi$ is a function of it. Overlap given the pair follows from positivity given $X$, because $P\{T{=}1 \mid \pi(X), \Psi(X)\}$ is an average of the true score $P\{T{=}1 \mid X\}$. Stratifying or matching on the pair therefore identifies the effect if either score is right, a matching counterpart of the double robustness of Chapter 11; @yang2023multiply build multiply robust matching estimators on this idea.
:::

### Matching under a Misspecified Score {#sec-w6-matching-misspec}

Weighting and matching use a fitted score in different ways. IPW uses its numerical *values*: the weight is $1/\tilde\pi$ or $\tilde\pi/(1-\tilde\pi)$, and wrong values generally give wrong weights and a wrong probability limit. There are exceptions. If the fitted logit differs from the true one by a constant, $\tilde\pi(X) = \expit\{\mathrm{logit}\,\pi(X) + c\}$, then every control odds weight is multiplied by $\exp(c)$:
$$\frac{\tilde\pi(X)}{1-\tilde\pi(X)} = \exp(c)\,\frac{\pi(X)}{1-\pi(X)},$$
and the common factor cancels in the Hájek ATT estimator, which is then exactly unchanged. Matching uses the score to decide *which units are alike*. The next lemma makes the identification part of this precise; write $\tilde b(X)$ for the limit of a fitted score, correct or not.

::: {#lem-matching-valid}
## When Matching on a Fitted Score Is Valid

Suppose $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$, and let $\tilde b(X)$ be any function of $X$. If $\pi(X)$ is a function of $\tilde b(X)$, or if some prognostic score is a function of $\tilde b(X)$, then $Y(0) \indep T \mid \tilde b(X)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

If $\pi(X) = g(\tilde b(X))$, then $P\{T{=}1 \mid X, \tilde b(X)\} = \pi(X) = g(\tilde b(X)) = P\{T{=}1 \mid \tilde b(X)\}$, so $\tilde b$ is a balancing score and the argument of @thm-ps applies. If $\Psi(X) = h(\tilde b(X))$ for a prognostic score $\Psi$, then $Y(0) \indep X \mid \Psi(X)$ implies $Y(0) \indep X \mid \{\Psi(X), \tilde b(X)\}$, that is, $Y(0) \indep X \mid \tilde b(X)$; so $\tilde b$ is a prognostic score and @thm-prognostic (i) applies.
:::

The lemma is an identification statement. Consistency of the matching estimator of the ATT needs more: overlap, smoothness of the conditional mean of $Y(0)$ in the score, match discrepancies that shrink as $n$ grows, and moment conditions. With these, the lemma gives the condition of Lesson 7 of the lab. The conditions of the lemma involve $\tilde b$ only through its level sets, the sets of units it treats as alike: if they hold for $\tilde b$, they hold for $g(\tilde b)$ for every one-to-one $g$. A misspecification that distorts the values of the score but keeps its level sets --- a wrong link, a miscalibrated fit, a monotone distortion of the fitted probabilities --- therefore leaves the identifying condition intact. It generally biases IPW, while matching on the fitted score can remain consistent.

The nearest-neighbor *algorithm* is not invariant in the same way, because it uses distances, and a one-to-one transformation can change them enough to change the match. Take a treated unit with score $0.50$ and two controls with scores $0.40$ and $0.59$. The distances are $0.10$ and $0.09$, so the match is $0.59$. Square all scores, a one-to-one map on $[0,1]$: the distances become $0.0900$ and $0.0981$, and the match becomes $0.40$. A fixed caliper is scale dependent for the same reason (@sec-w6-caliper). A transformation that keeps the level sets changes which matches are made in a finite sample, not the identifying condition; stratification on quantiles of the score is exactly invariant.

Misspecifications that keep the level sets are common. If $\pi(X) = F(\beta^\top X)$ for an increasing link $F$ and $X$ is Gaussian, or more generally elliptically symmetric, the logistic maximum-likelihood fit converges to $\expit(a + c\beta^\top X)$ for some constants $a$ and $c$, with $c > 0$ unless the fit is degenerate [@li1989regression]: the fitted score is then a monotone function of the true one, whatever $F$ is. @waernbaum2012model studies such robustness classes for matching and compares them with doubly robust estimation.

The protection has limits. A misspecification that merges units with different true scores *and* different prognoses satisfies neither condition of the lemma, and then matching is biased along with IPW. Matching is more robust than IPW in a specific sense: its identifying condition survives a larger class of misspecifications, not all of them, and consistency still needs the regularity conditions above.

::: {#exm-matching-misspec}
## Two Misspecifications

Let $X$ have three independent $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$ components and $\tau(X) = 1 + 0.5X_1$. In design A the true score has a complementary log-log link, $\pi(X) = 1 - \exp[-\exp\{-0.8 + 0.6X_1 + 0.4X_2 - 0.3X_3\}]$, and $m_0(X) = X_1^2 + X_2 + \exp(0.5X_3)$; the logistic fit has the wrong link but the right index. In design B the true score is U-shaped, $\pi(X) = \expit(-1 + 0.9X_1^2 + 0.3X_2)$, and $m_0(X) = X_1^2 + X_2$; the linear logistic fit merges units with $X_1$ and $-X_1$, which differ in score and in prognosis. With $n = 2{,}000$ and $1{,}000$ replications (script `robmatch.R`, seed 6), the biases (SDs) for the ATT are:

|  | **True score** |  | **Logistic fit** |  |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Design** | Hájek ATT | NNM | Hájek ATT | NNM |
| A: wrong link | $0.012$ $(0.246)$ | $0.034$ $(0.164)$ | $0.177$ $(0.110)$ | $0.037$ $(0.155)$ |
| B: merged level sets | $0.100$ $(0.481)$ | $0.111$ $(0.144)$ | $1.095$ $(0.083)$ | $1.089$ $(0.097)$ |

In design A, $X$ is Gaussian and the true score is an increasing function of the index $0.6X_1 + 0.4X_2 - 0.3X_3$, so by @li1989regression the limit of the logistic fit is an increasing function of the true score: in the population the fit keeps the level sets exactly, and the first condition of the lemma holds. (The finite-sample rank correlation between the fitted and the true score is $0.9999$.) Matching on the fit behaves like matching on the true score. The fitted logit is not the true logit plus a constant, so the exception above does not apply, and the Hájek estimator is biased here by $0.177$, about $50$ Monte Carlo standard errors. In design B the rank correlation is $0.41$ and both estimators fail. (The true-score rows of design B carry some finite-sample bias from thin overlap at large $|X_1|$; the contrast is $0.1$ against $1.1$.) The table illustrates the lemma; it does not prove consistency, which rests on the lemma and the regularity conditions.
:::

Part 2 of the lab (@sec-w6-lab-part2) lies between the two designs, and the second condition of the lemma offers an explanation after one reduction. In the lab the five covariates are independent $\mathrm{N}(0,1)$ and the error is independent of them; in Part 2, $X_2$ and $X_3$ affect only the outcome. Let $Z = (X_1, X_4, X_5)$. Treatment depends on $X$ only through $Z$, so $Y(0) \indep T \mid Z$ and $Z$ is a sufficient adjustment set. Given $Z$, the outcome-only terms $0.5X_2 + 0.4X_3$ join $\varepsilon$ in a residual that is independent of $(Z, T)$, so
$$Y(0) = 8 + r(Z) + (0.5X_2 + 0.4X_3 + \varepsilon), \qquad r(Z) = 0.8X_1 + 0.3X_4 + 0.2X_5,$$
and $r(Z)$ is a prognostic score relative to $Z$: $Y(0) \indep Z \mid r(Z)$. (It is not a prognostic score relative to $X$, because the law of $Y(0)$ given $r$ still depends on $X_2$ and $X_3$.) Applied with $Z$ in place of $X$, the lemma covers any fitted score that determines $r(Z)$, such as an increasing function of $r(Z)$. The misspecified linear fit does not keep the level sets of the true score (rank correlation $0.83$), but its index, approximately $0.64X_1 + 0.19X_4 + 0.10X_5$ with negligible coefficients on $X_2$ and $X_3$, has correlation $0.994$ with $r(Z)$: the fitted score is nearly a prognostic score for $Z$. This helps explain why NNM has a small bias in this simulation ($0.020$, against $0.154$ for the Hájek ATT). A correlation of $0.994$ is not an exact robustness guarantee and gives no bound on the bias.

## Inverse Probability Weighting {#sec-w6-ipw}

### The IPW Identification Formula {#sec-w6-ipw-formula}

The ATE admits an alternative representation as an *inverse probability weighting* (IPW) formula, in which each observed outcome is weighted by the inverse probability of the treatment actually received. The survey analogy is exact: the treated arm is a sample from the population of all $n$ units with known inclusion probabilities $\pi(X_i)$, and the Horvitz--Thompson estimator is the natural tool. The precise statement, arm by arm:

::: {#thm-ipw}
## IPW Identification

Fix $t \in \{0, 1\}$ and assume: (i) *consistency*: $T = t$ implies $Y = Y(t)$; (ii) *weak conditional exchangeability*: $Y(t) \indep T \mid X$; (iii) *positivity*: $P(T{=}t \mid X) > 0$ almost surely; and (iv) *integrability*: $\E|Y(t)| < \infty$. Then
$$\E\!\left[\frac{T \cdot Y}{\pi(X)}\right] = \E[Y(1)] \;\;\text{for } t = 1, \qquad \E\!\left[\frac{(1-T) \cdot Y}{1 - \pi(X)}\right] = \E[Y(0)] \;\;\text{for } t = 0.$$
If the conditions hold for both treatment levels,
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E\!\left[\frac{T \cdot Y}{\pi(X)} - \frac{(1-T) \cdot Y}{1 - \pi(X)}\right].$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

$$\E\!\left[\frac{T Y}{\pi(X)}\right] = \E\!\left[\frac{T\, Y(1)}{\pi(X)}\right] = \E\!\left[\frac{Y(1)}{\pi(X)}\, \E\bigl[T \mid X,\, Y(1)\bigr]\right] = \E\!\left[\frac{Y(1)}{\pi(X)}\, \pi(X)\right] = \E[Y(1)].$$
The first equality uses consistency ($Y = Y(1)$ when $T{=}1$). The second is the law of iterated expectations conditioning on $(X, Y(1))$; the factor $Y(1)/\pi(X)$ is measurable with respect to the conditioning variables and pulls out of the inner expectation. The third uses ignorability: $Y(1) \indep T \mid X$ implies $\E[T \mid X, Y(1)] = \E[T \mid X] = \pi(X)$. Integrability, with positivity, ensures each expectation is well defined. The case $t = 0$ is symmetric, and subtracting the two identities gives the ATE formula.
:::

In the running example, the treated arm of cell $(0,0)$ has $80$ units and weight $1/0.2 = 5$, so it stands in for all $400$ units of that cell; the $160$ treated units of cell $(1,1)$ have weight $1.25$ and stand in for $200$. Each reweighted arm reproduces the population cell counts, and then $\E\{TY/\pi(X)\} = \sum_x P(x)\,\pi(x)\,\mu(1,x)/\pi(x) = \sum_x P(x)\mu(1,x) = 7.6$, $\E\{Y(0)\} = 5.2$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = 2.4$. The idealized table has $N_{1x} = N_x\pi(x)$ exactly; with random assignment the weighted counts match the population counts in expectation, which is the content of @lem-weighted-balance below.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Scope of the Ignorability Assumption Used

@thm-ipw is deliberately stated arm by arm under the *marginal* independence $Y(t) \indep T \mid X$, not the full joint independence $(Y(0), Y(1)) \indep T \mid X$: each per-arm identity needs only the corresponding marginal condition together with arm-specific positivity. The joint independence is invoked throughout this chapter for stylistic uniformity with the back-door theorem of Chapter 5 and because joint-distribution targets such as $\mathrm{Var}\{Y(1) - Y(0)\}$ at least require it --- although even joint ignorability identifies only the two marginal potential-outcome distributions, not the cross-world dependence between $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$, so such targets remain only partially identified without further assumptions (Chapter 4). The marginal version suffices for any estimand expressible as a contrast of marginal means.
:::

### Why the Weights Work: Weighted-Balance Identities {#sec-w6-weighted-balance}

The balancing theorem and the IPW formula are two faces of the same mechanism, and the connection can be made algebraic: inverse-probability weights re-create, inside each treatment arm, the covariate distribution of the target population.

::: {#lem-weighted-balance}
## Weighted-Balance Identities

Let $h(X)$ be any integrable function of the covariates and suppose $0 < \pi(X) < 1$ almost surely. Then
$$\E\!\left[\frac{T\, h(X)}{\pi(X)}\right] = \E[h(X)] \qquad\text{and}\qquad \E\!\left[\frac{(1-T)\, h(X)}{1-\pi(X)}\right] = \E[h(X)].$$
Moreover, for the treated target population,
$$\frac{1}{P(T{=}1)}\, \E\!\left[(1-T)\,\frac{\pi(X)}{1-\pi(X)}\, h(X)\right] = \E\bigl[h(X) \mid T{=}1\bigr].$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

For the first identity, condition on $X$ and note that $h(X)/\pi(X)$ pulls out of the inner expectation: $\E[T h(X)/\pi(X)] = \E\bigl[h(X)\,\E(T \mid X)/\pi(X)\bigr] = \E[h(X)]$. The second is symmetric. For the third,
$$\E\!\left[(1-T)\,\frac{\pi(X)}{1-\pi(X)}\, h(X)\right] = \E\!\left[\bigl\{1 - \pi(X)\bigr\}\, \frac{\pi(X)}{1-\pi(X)}\, h(X)\right] = \E\bigl[\pi(X)\, h(X)\bigr] = \E\bigl[T\, h(X)\bigr],$$
and $\E[T\, h(X)] = P(T{=}1)\,\E[h(X) \mid T{=}1]$.
:::

Taking $h \equiv 1$ shows that each arm's inverse-weight total, divided by the full sample size $n$, has expectation one --- the weight-sum quantities $w_T$ and $w_C$ of the next subsection. Taking $h(X) = X_j$ shows that the weighted treated and control samples reproduce the covariate means of the target population: the full population under the ATE weights $1/\pi(X)$ and $1/\{1-\pi(X)\}$, the treated subpopulation under the ATT odds weights $\pi(X)/\{1-\pi(X)\}$ applied to the control arm. This is why the weights take their particular forms.
