Note that no potential outcomes appear in the lemma: like the balancing theorem, it is a property of the assignment mechanism alone. @thm-ipw is the step from $h(X)$ to $Y(1)$: the target is $\E\{Y(1)\}$, not $\E(Y)$; ignorability turns $\E\{TY(1)/\pi(X)\}$ into $\E[\pi(X)\E\{Y(1)\mid X\}/\pi(X)]$, and consistency replaces $TY(1)$ by the observed $TY$.

Dividing the third identity by its $h \equiv 1$ case, $\E\{(1-T)\,o(X)\} = P(T{=}1)$ with $o(X) = \pi(X)/\{1-\pi(X)\}$, gives the normalized balance identity
$$\frac{\E\{o(X)\,h(X) \mid T{=}0\}}{\E\{o(X) \mid T{=}0\}} = \E\{h(X) \mid T{=}1\} \qquad\text{for every integrable } h(X):$$ {#eq-w6-att-balance}
ideal odds weighting balances *every* function of $X$ between the weighted controls and the treated population --- the covariates, their squares and products, and any prognostic function such as $m_0(X) = \E\{Y(0) \mid X\}$ or $P(Y(0) > t \mid X)$ (@sec-w6-prognostic) --- and no causal assumption is involved. The left side is the Hájek form. @eq-w6-att-balance is a population identity under the true odds, not a sample guarantee: a fitted score balances none of these functions exactly in a realized sample, and no sample can balance all of them. Which functions to balance is a design choice, which @sec-w6-calibration makes by calibration, with prognostic functions as the natural candidates.

The one choice of $h$ that needs ignorability is $h = Y(0)$, and it identifies the ATT.

::: {#cor-ipw-att}
## IPW Identification of the ATT

Assume consistency, $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$, control-arm positivity $\pi(X) < 1$ almost surely, and $\E|Y(0)| < \infty$. Then
$$\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\} = \frac{\E\{o(X)\,Y \mid T{=}0\}}{\E\{o(X) \mid T{=}0\}}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = \E(Y \mid T{=}1) - \frac{\E\{o(X)\,Y \mid T{=}0\}}{\E\{o(X) \mid T{=}0\}}.$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

The treated mean needs consistency only: $\E\{Y(1) \mid T{=}1\} = \E(Y \mid T{=}1)$. For the control mean, apply @eq-w6-att-balance with $h(X) = m_0(X) = \E\{Y(0) \mid X\}$ and then use ignorability, $\E\{Y(0) \mid X\} = \E\{Y(0) \mid X, T{=}t\}$ for $t = 0, 1$, once on each side. On the right, $\E\{m_0(X) \mid T{=}1\} = \E[\E\{Y(0) \mid X, T{=}1\} \mid T{=}1] = \E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\}$. On the left, since $o(X)$ is a function of $X$,
$$\begin{aligned} \E\{o(X)\,m_0(X) \mid T{=}0\} &= \E\bigl[o(X)\,\E\{Y(0) \mid X, T{=}0\} \bigm| T{=}0\bigr]\\ &= \E\bigl[o(X)\,\E(Y \mid X, T{=}0) \bigm| T{=}0\bigr] = \E\{o(X)\,Y \mid T{=}0\}, \end{aligned}$$
using consistency in the middle step and iterated expectations within the control arm in the last. Substituting both into @eq-w6-att-balance gives the first display; subtracting from the treated mean gives the second.
:::

Ignorability enters only to replace $m_0(X)$ by arm-specific conditional means; the balancing itself is @eq-w6-att-balance. The right side of the first display is the population version of the Hájek-ATT estimator of @sec-w6-ht-hajek.

Compared with the ATE, one arm is reweighted rather than two, the assumptions are one-sided --- $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$ and $\pi(X) < 1$, so the ATT survives regions where $\pi(x) = 0$ (@sec-w6-retargeting) --- and the target population is $X \mid T{=}1$, whose law has density $\pi(x)f_X(x)/P(T{=}1)$. In the running example, the odds $(0.25, 1, 1, 4)$ applied to the control counts $(320, 100, 100, 40)$ give weighted counts $(80, 100, 100, 160) = N_{1x}$, so $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\} = 2720/440 = 68/11$, $\E(Y \mid T{=}1) = 98/11$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = 30/11$. The ATC is the mirror image.

### The Horvitz--Thompson and Hájek Estimators {#sec-w6-ht-hajek}

Write $\hat\pi_i = \hat\pi(X_i)$ and define the inverse-probability weights $a_i = T_i/\hat\pi_i$ and $c_i = (1-T_i)/(1-\hat\pi_i)$. The sample analogue of @thm-ipw is the *Horvitz--Thompson* (HT) IPW estimator:
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (a_i - c_i)\,Y_i = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[\frac{T_i Y_i}{\hat\pi(X_i)} - \frac{(1-T_i) Y_i}{1-\hat\pi(X_i)}\right].$$
This estimator is consistent when $\hat\pi(X)$ converges to $\pi(X)$, given positivity and mild moment conditions --- with flexible nuisance estimators evaluated on the same sample, additional conditions such as sample splitting may be required (Chapter 12) --- but it can be *inefficient* due to extreme weights. In practice, a fitted score used for weighting is evaluated through weighted covariate balance, the weight distribution, and effective sample sizes (@sec-w6-balance-diagnostics and @sec-w6-design-workflow). The *normalized* (Hájek) estimator divides by the sum of weights within each group:
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}} = \frac{\sum_i a_i Y_i}{\sum_i a_i} - \frac{\sum_i c_i Y_i}{\sum_i c_i} = \frac{\sum_i T_i Y_i / \hat\pi(X_i)}{\sum_i T_i / \hat\pi(X_i)} - \frac{\sum_i (1-T_i) Y_i / (1-\hat\pi(X_i))}{\sum_i (1-T_i) / (1-\hat\pi(X_i))}.$$
The same two forms exist for the ATT: the treated arm needs no weight, and a control receives the odds $o_i = \hat\pi_i/(1-\hat\pi_i)$,
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT,ATT}} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=1} Y_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=0} o_iY_i, \qquad \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ,ATT}} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=1} Y_i - \frac{\sum_{i:\,T_i=0} o_iY_i}{\sum_{i:\,T_i=0} o_i}.$$
Both pairs are consistent for their targets under positivity and moment conditions; in finite samples they can differ a great deal.

**Why Hájek: one identity.** Let $w_T = n^{-1}\sum_i a_i$ and $w_C = n^{-1}\sum_i c_i$, each arm's inverse-weight total divided by $n$. By @lem-weighted-balance with $h \equiv 1$, each has expectation one under the true score, but each fluctuates. Shifting every outcome by a constant $c$ gives
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(Y + c) = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(Y) + c\,(w_T - w_C), \qquad \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}}(Y + c) = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}}(Y).$$ {#eq-w6-shift}
HT inherits the fluctuation of $w_T - w_C$, multiplied by the level of the outcome; Hájek is location invariant because each arm's self-normalized mean shifts by exactly $c$. A unit with $\pi(X_i) = 0.05$ has weight $20$; with an outcome near a baseline of $8$, its contribution to the HT sum is of order $160$, and which units are extreme varies across samples. Normalization makes the estimate invariant to the outcome origin and often improves stability, which is why the Hájek form is the recommended default; but a single unit can still carry most of an arm's weight, so extreme weights remain a problem for both estimators. The same holds for the ATT: the odds weight $0.95/0.05 = 19$ on a control with a high score is as explosive as the ATE weight.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Normalization Is Not a Universal Improvement

@eq-w6-shift shows that HT *need not* be location invariant, not that Hájek always has the smaller variance. Let $Y(1) = \pi(X)$ and $Y(0) = \pi(X) - 1$. Then every unit contributes exactly $1$ to the known-score HT estimator, $T_iY_i/\pi_i - (1-T_i)Y_i/(1-\pi_i) = T_i + (1-T_i) = 1$, so $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = 1$ with zero variance, while the Hájek estimator varies from sample to sample. There is no universal variance ordering. In the special case of a constant score $\pi(X) = p$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}}$ reduces exactly to the difference in arm means, whereas $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$ does so only when the realized count satisfies $n_1 = np$ (Problem 2).
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: The Saturated Score --- an Exact Finite-Sample Case

Suppose $X$ is discrete with cells $x$, and let $\hat\pi(x) = n_{1x}/n_x$ be the within-cell treated proportion, the maximum-likelihood fit of the saturated logistic model. Whenever every cell contains both arms,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{T_i}{\hat\pi(X_i)} = \sum_x n_{1x}\,\frac{n_x}{n_{1x}} = n, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1-T_i}{1-\hat\pi(X_i)} = \sum_x n_{0x}\,\frac{n_x}{n_{0x}} = n,$$
so $w_T = w_C = 1$ in every such sample, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}}$, and both equal the standardization estimator $\sum_x (n_x/n)(\bar Y_{1,x} - \bar Y_{0,x})$ of Chapter 5. The estimated score replaced the known assignment probability by the *realized* treated fraction of each cell, so the reweighted arm reproduces the sample's cell counts exactly rather than in expectation, and the chance imbalance that drives the known-score variance is removed. Exact cell balance is a property of the saturated fit; an ordinary logistic fit on $(1, X)$ does not make the IPW arms balance $X$ exactly. The general phenomenon --- an estimated score that improves on the true one --- is asymptotic and is the subject of the next subsection.
:::

### Why an Estimated Score Can Be More Precise Than the True One {#sec-w6-estimated-score}

Replacing the true score by a maximum-likelihood estimate from a correctly specified model does not merely preserve the precision of IPW; it improves it. The argument has the nuisance-parameter structure of Chapter 5, with one twist in the sign.

**Setting.** The observations $(T_i, X_i, Y_i)$ are i.i.d.; the score follows a correctly specified smooth parametric model $\pi(X;\gamma)$, logistic for instance, with true value $\gamma_0$, fitted by regular maximum likelihood on the same sample with nonsingular information; and $\E[Y(1)^2/\pi(X) + Y(0)^2/\{1-\pi(X)\}] < \infty$. Let $S_i = \partial \log p(T_i \mid X_i;\gamma_0)/\partial\gamma$ be the *likelihood score vector* --- not the propensity score; the two meanings of "score" are both in play here --- and $\mathcal{I} = \E(S S^\top)$ the information. Write
$$\varphi_i(\gamma) = \frac{T_iY_i}{\pi(X_i;\gamma)} - \frac{(1-T_i)Y_i}{1-\pi(X_i;\gamma)} - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}, \qquad \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(\hat\gamma) - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i(\hat\gamma).$$

**Expansion in the nuisance.** Linearizing in $\gamma$,
$$\sqrt n\,\{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(\hat\gamma) - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}\} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i(\gamma_0)}_{\text{known-score term}} + \underbrace{\Gamma\,\sqrt n\,(\hat\gamma - \gamma_0)}_{\text{estimation error}} + o_p(1), \qquad \Gamma = \E\{\partial\varphi(\gamma_0)/\partial\gamma^\top\},$$
and the maximum-likelihood expansion gives $\sqrt n(\hat\gamma - \gamma_0) = \mathcal{I}^{-1} n^{-1/2}\sum_i S_i + o_p(1)$. In Chapter 5 the estimation error of the outcome-regression coefficient was uncorrelated with the sampling error and added variance. Here the two terms are negatively related: the estimation error subtracts a piece of the known-score term.

::: {#thm-estimated-score}
## Variance Reduction from an Estimated Score

Under the setting above, $\Gamma = -\E(\varphi S^\top)$, the influence function of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(\hat\gamma)$ is
$$\psi = \varphi - \E(\varphi S^\top)\,\mathcal{I}^{-1} S = \varphi - \Pi(\varphi \mid S),$$
$\varphi$ minus its linear projection on the likelihood score vector, and the limiting variances of the $\sqrt n$-scaled estimators satisfy
$$V_{\mathrm{est}} = \mathrm{Var}(\varphi) - \E(\varphi S^\top)\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}\,\E(S\varphi) \;\le\; V_{\mathrm{known}} = \mathrm{Var}(\varphi), \qquad \mathrm{Var}\{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(\hat\gamma)\} \approx V_{\mathrm{est}}/n.$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

Let $\E_\gamma$ denote expectation when the conditional law of $T$ given $X$ is $\pi(X;\gamma)$, the law of $(X, Y(0), Y(1))$ being fixed. @thm-ipw applied at each $\gamma$ gives $\E_\gamma\{\varphi(\gamma)\} = 0$ for *every* $\gamma$. Differentiating under the integral sign, justified by the regularity of the model, and using $\partial p(T\mid X;\gamma)/\partial\gamma = p\,S^\top$,
$$0 = \frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma^\top}\, \E_\gamma\{\varphi(\gamma)\}\Big|_{\gamma_0} = \E\Bigl\{\frac{\partial\varphi(\gamma_0)}{\partial\gamma^\top}\Bigr\} + \E\bigl\{\varphi(\gamma_0)\,S^\top\bigr\},$$
the generalized information equality, so $\Gamma = -\E(\varphi S^\top)$. Substituting into the expansion, $\sqrt n\{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}(\hat\gamma) - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}\} = n^{-1/2}\sum_i \{\varphi_i - \E(\varphi S^\top)\mathcal{I}^{-1}S_i\} + o_p(1)$, whose summands are the residuals of $\varphi$ after linear projection on $S$. The variance of a residual is the variance of $\varphi$ minus the variance of the projection, $\E(\varphi S^\top)\mathcal{I}^{-1}\E(S\varphi) \ge 0$.
:::

For the logistic model with regressors $f(X)$, $S_i = \{T_i - \pi(X_i)\}f(X_i)$, and the likelihood equations $\sum_i\{T_i - \hat\pi(X_i)\}f(X_i) = 0$ hold exactly in the sample. They act as *control variates*: the part of the IPW error that is correlated with $\{T - \pi(X)\}f(X)$ is removed, and the proportional variance reduction $1 - V_{\mathrm{est}}/V_{\mathrm{known}}$ is the squared multiple correlation of $\varphi$ with the components of $S$. The remark on the saturated score is the extreme case, in which the removal is exact in every sample; in the lab below, the estimated score cuts the standard deviation of HT-ATE from $0.626$ to $0.194$. The gain requires a correctly specified score fitted by maximum likelihood (or a suitable nonparametric fit; the semiparametric efficiency result is @hirano2003efficient); it does not hold for an arbitrary estimate of $\pi$, and it says nothing about misspecification, which removes the consistency guarantee altogether (Part 2 of the lab).

**Variance estimation.** With $\hat\varphi_i = \varphi_i(\hat\gamma)$ evaluated at $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat S_i$ the fitted likelihood score vector, $\hat{\mathcal I} = n^{-1}\sum_i \hat S_i\hat S_i^\top$, and $\hat\Gamma = n^{-1}\sum_i \hat\varphi_i\hat S_i^\top$, the influence-function plug-in is
$$\hat\psi_i = \hat\varphi_i - \hat\Gamma\,\hat{\mathcal I}^{-1}\hat S_i, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\psi_i^2,$$
an estimate of $V_{\mathrm{est}}/n$ under the stated model; using $\hat\varphi_i$ alone, as if the score were known, is asymptotically conservative. For the Hájek estimator, a ratio in each arm, linearize as in Chapter 5 by centering each arm at its Hájek mean, $\hat\varphi_{\mathrm{HJ},i} = T_i(Y_i - \hat\mu_1)/\hat\pi_i - (1-T_i)(Y_i - \hat\mu_0)/(1-\hat\pi_i)$ with no further $-\hat\tau$, and project on $\hat S_i$ as before. These are large-sample statements, not finite-sample guarantees. The bootstrap is also available for these regular parametric estimators: resample units and *refit* $\hat\pi$ in every replication, since treating $\hat\pi$ as fixed overstates the variance. With flexible or adaptive fitting methods, bootstrap validity needs separate justification, and for matching estimators the ordinary bootstrap fails.

### Advanced Topic: Calibrated Estimation of the Propensity Score {#sec-w6-calibration}

Maximum likelihood is not the only way to fit the score. The calibration approach of @tan2020regularized fits the same logistic model so that the inverse-probability weights balance the covariates *exactly* in the sample. Tan's loss is easiest to understand as the dual of a calibration problem posed by @wang2025information. The construction is the survey calibration of Chapter 5 [@deville1992calibration] with the treated arm as the sample and the whole data set as the population. With the control arm as the sample and the treated arm as the population, the same construction gives the ATT calibration known as entropy balancing, later in the section.

**The primal problem.** Let $S = \{i : T_i = 1\}$ and $f_i = f(X_i)$ with $f(X) = (1, X^\top)^\top$. Choose weights $\{\omega_i\}_{i \in S}$ and estimate $\E\{Y(1)\}$ by $n^{-1}\sum_{i \in S}\omega_i Y_i$. @wang2025information choose the weights to solve
$$\min_{\omega}\ \sum_{i\in S} (\omega_i - 1)\{\log(\omega_i - 1) - 1\} \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \sum_{i\in S}\omega_i f_i = \sum_{i=1}^n f_i$$ {#eq-w6-cal-primal}
over $\omega_i > 1$. The constraint is exact covariate balance: the reweighted treated arm reproduces the sample totals of $f(X)$, the sample version of the first identity in @lem-weighted-balance. The objective is a shifted Kullback--Leibler entropy, and the shift has a direct reading. With $r_i = \omega_i - 1$, the problem is to minimize $\sum_{i\in S}(r_i\log r_i - r_i)$ subject to $\sum_{i\in S} r_i f_i = \sum_{i:\,T_i=0} f_i$: each treated unit keeps a weight of one for itself, and the excess weights $r_i$, as close to one as possible in Kullback--Leibler divergence, make the treated arm reproduce the control totals as well.

Write $G(\omega) = (\omega-1)\{\log(\omega-1)-1\}$, so that $G'(\omega) = \log(\omega - 1)$, and introduce a multiplier $\lambda$ for the constraint. Differentiating the Lagrangian $L(\omega,\lambda) = \sum_{i\in S}G(\omega_i) - \lambda^\top(\sum_{i\in S}\omega_i f_i - \sum_{i=1}^n f_i)$ with respect to $\omega_i$ gives $\log(\omega_i - 1) = \lambda^\top f_i$, so
$$\hat\omega_i(\lambda) = 1 + \exp(\lambda^\top f_i) = \frac{1}{\expit(-\lambda^\top f_i)} = \frac{1}{\pi(X_i;\gamma)}, \qquad \gamma = -\lambda,$$
the inverse of a *logistic* propensity score: the model is implied by the objective, not assumed.

**The dual problem is Tan's calibration loss.** Substituting $\hat\omega_i(\lambda)$ back into $L$ leaves a problem in the low-dimensional $\lambda$ alone. With $u_i = \lambda^\top f_i$ and $\hat\omega_i - 1 = \exp(u_i)$,
$$G(\hat\omega_i) - u_i\,\hat\omega_i = \exp(u_i)(u_i - 1) - u_i\{1 + \exp(u_i)\} = -u_i - \exp(u_i),$$
so $L\{\hat\omega(\lambda),\lambda\} = -F(\lambda)$ with
$$F(\lambda) = \sum_{i\in S}\{\lambda^\top f_i + \exp(\lambda^\top f_i)\} - \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda^\top f_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \Bigl[T_i \exp\{-\gamma^\top f_i\} + (1 - T_i)\,\gamma^\top f_i\Bigr] = \ell_{\mathrm{CAL}}(\gamma),$$ {#eq-w6-tan-loss}
the calibration loss of @tan2020regularized. $F$ is convex, and $\hat\lambda$ minimizes it. Its gradient vanishes if and only if $\sum_i T_i f_i/\hat\pi_i = \sum_i f_i$, the primal constraint: exact balance is not a by-product of this fit, it is what the weights were chosen to satisfy. Because $f$ contains the constant, $\sum_i T_i/\hat\pi_i = n$, so the Horvitz--Thompson and Hájek estimators coincide. Logistic maximum likelihood minimizes $-\sum_i\{T_i\log\pi_i + (1-T_i)\log(1-\pi_i)\}$ instead; its score equation $\sum_i(T_i - \hat\pi_i)f_i = 0$ balances only on the probability scale. The control arm is handled by the mirror-image loss $\sum_i[(1-T_i)\exp\{\gamma^\top f_i\} - T_i\,\gamma^\top f_i]$, whose first-order condition is $\sum_i(1-T_i)f_i/(1-\hat\pi_i) = \sum_i f_i$; it returns below as the dual of the ATT calibration.

::: {#prp-cal-dr}
## What Exact Balance Buys

Suppose $\E\{Y(1) \mid X\} = \beta^\top f(X)$ for some $\beta$, and let $\hat\omega_i$ be weights that satisfy the constraint of @eq-w6-cal-primal --- the calibrated weights in particular --- with $\hat\omega_i \to \omega^*(X_i)$ uniformly for some function $\omega^*$. Under consistency, $Y(1) \indep T \mid X$, and moment conditions, $n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}\hat\omega_i Y_i \pto \E\{Y(1)\}$ whether or not the logistic score model implied by the weights is correct.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse=true icon=false}
## Proof (second reading)

Write $\varepsilon_i = Y_i(1) - \beta^\top f_i$, so $\E(\varepsilon \mid X) = 0$. By the constraint,
$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i\in S}\hat\omega_i Y_i = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \beta^\top f_i + \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n T_i\,\hat\omega_i\,\varepsilon_i .$$
The first term converges to $\E\{\beta^\top f(X)\} = \E\{Y(1)\}$. In the second, replace $\hat\omega_i$ by $\omega^*(X_i)$ at the cost of an $o_p(1)$ term; then $\E\{T\,\omega^*(X)\,\varepsilon\} = \E[\omega^*(X)\,\pi(X)\,\E\{\varepsilon \mid X, T{=}1\}] = \E[\omega^*(X)\,\pi(X)\,\E(\varepsilon \mid X)] = 0$, using $Y(1) \indep T \mid X$ in the middle step. The argument used only the balance constraint and the outcome model, not the correctness of the weights' functional form.
:::

Together with the usual IPW argument --- if the implied score model is correct, the weights converge to the true inverse probabilities and consistency follows from @thm-ipw --- this is the double robustness of Chapter 11, obtained here at the fitting stage of the score rather than by augmenting the estimator. The balanced weights annihilate the linear part of the outcome, and the residual term has mean zero under unconfoundedness whatever $\hat\pi$ converges to: the Chapter 5 argument for regression weights once more.

**Calibration for the ATT.** For the ATT only the control mean $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\}$ needs weighting, and the population identity to reproduce in the sample is the third one in @lem-weighted-balance, in its unnormalized form $\E\{(1-T)\,o(X)\,h(X)\} = \E\{T\,h(X)\}$ with $o(X) = \pi(X)/\{1-\pi(X)\}$. Applied to $h = f$, it calibrates the control arm to the treated totals. Let $S_0 = \{i : T_i = 0\}$, and estimate $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\}$ by $n_1^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_0}\omega_i Y_i$, with weights solving
$$\min_{\omega}\ \sum_{i\in S_0} (\omega_i\log\omega_i - \omega_i) \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \sum_{i\in S_0}\omega_i f_i = \sum_{i:\,T_i=1} f_i$$ {#eq-w6-att-primal}
over $\omega_i > 0$. The objective is the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the weights from the unit weight, up to an additive constant, now without the shift: the ideal ATT weights are the odds, with no unit of weight reserved for the control itself. Stationarity of the Lagrangian gives $\log\omega_i = \lambda^\top f_i$, so $\hat\omega_i = \exp(\lambda^\top f_i) = \pi(X_i;\gamma)/\{1 - \pi(X_i;\gamma)\}$ with $\gamma = \lambda$, the odds under a logistic score. With $G(\omega) = \omega\log\omega - \omega$, $G(\hat\omega_i) - \lambda^\top f_i\,\hat\omega_i = -\exp(\lambda^\top f_i)$, and the dual objective is
$$F(\lambda) = \sum_{i\in S_0}\exp(\lambda^\top f_i) - \sum_{i:\,T_i=1}\lambda^\top f_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \Bigl[(1 - T_i)\exp\{\gamma^\top f_i\} - T_i\,\gamma^\top f_i\Bigr],$$ {#eq-w6-att-dual}
which is exactly the control-arm loss of the ATE. Its gradient vanishes if and only if the constraint of @eq-w6-att-primal holds. Because $f$ contains the constant, $\sum_{i\in S_0}\hat\omega_i = n_1$, so the Horvitz--Thompson and Hájek forms of the ATT estimator coincide, as they did for the ATE.

The coincidence of the two losses is the identity $1/(1-\pi) = 1 + \pi/(1-\pi)$. The ATE control-arm constraint $\sum_{i\in S_0}\{1 + \exp(\gamma^\top f_i)\}f_i = \sum_{i=1}^n f_i$ becomes, after $\sum_{i\in S_0} f_i$ is subtracted from both sides, the ATT constraint $\sum_{i\in S_0}\exp(\gamma^\top f_i)f_i = \sum_{i:\,T_i=1} f_i$. The two fits therefore share $\hat\gamma$, and on the controls $\hat\omega_i^{\mathrm{ATE}} = 1 + \hat\omega_i^{\mathrm{ATT}}$: one fit calibrates both weighting schemes. The shift by one in the objective of @eq-w6-cal-primal is this identity.

**Entropy balancing.** @hainmueller2012entropy proposed exactly @eq-w6-att-primal, up to the normalization of the weights: choose the control weights closest to uniform in Kullback--Leibler divergence subject to reproducing the treated moments of $f(X)$. The logistic form of the odds is implied by the objective, not assumed, and @zhao2017entropy identify the dual @eq-w6-att-dual and prove the double robustness stated next. Two practical points follow from the form of the weights. They are positive by construction, unlike the regression weights of Chapter 5, which can be negative. And positive weights that satisfy the constraint exist only if the treated mean of the covariates lies inside the convex hull of the control covariate values; when it does not, the dual @eq-w6-att-dual is unbounded below and has no minimizer. This is the sample-level face of an ATT overlap failure, $\pi(x)$ near one where the treated units are (@sec-w6-retargeting).

**What exact balance buys for the ATT.** The analogue of @prp-cal-dr holds with one-sided assumptions. Suppose $\E\{Y(0) \mid X\} = \beta^\top f(X)$, let $\hat\omega_i$ be weights that satisfy the constraint of @eq-w6-att-primal, with a uniform limit $\omega^*(X_i)$, and assume consistency, $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$, $P(T{=}1) > 0$, and moment conditions. Write $\varepsilon_i = Y_i(0) - \beta^\top f_i$, so that $Y_i = \beta^\top f_i + \varepsilon_i$ for the controls. By the constraint,
$$\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i\in S_0}\hat\omega_i Y_i = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=1}\beta^\top f_i + \frac{n}{n_1}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (1-T_i)\,\hat\omega_i\, \varepsilon_i .$$
The first term converges to $\E\{m_0(X) \mid T{=}1\} = \E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\}$, by ignorability as in the proof of @cor-ipw-att. In the second, $n/n_1 \to 1/P(T{=}1)$, and $\E\{(1-T)\,\omega^*(X)\,\varepsilon\} = \E[\omega^*(X)\{1-\pi(X)\} \E(\varepsilon \mid X, T{=}0)] = 0$, because $\E(\varepsilon \mid X, T{=}0) = \E(\varepsilon \mid X) = 0$ under $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$. Hence the calibrated estimator of $\E\{Y(0) \mid T{=}1\}$ is consistent if the outcome model for $Y(0)$ is linear in $f$; if instead the logistic score is correct, $\hat\omega_i \to o(X_i)$ and @cor-ipw-att applies. Only the control-arm outcome model and $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$ enter, matching the one-sided assumptions of the ATT.

::: {#exm-cal-lab}
## The Calibration Loss on the Lab's Misspecified Design

Part 2 of the lab (@sec-w6-lab-part2) fits a linear logistic model to a treatment mechanism that is quadratic in $X_1$, while the outcome is linear in $X$. Fitting the *same* linear logit by the calibration loss instead of maximum likelihood, in a separate run of $1{,}000$ replications at $n = 1{,}000$ (script `cal18.R`, seed 18), gives the following for the ATE, whose true value is $1$, and for the ATT, whose true value is $1.152$. The ATT row of the calibration uses the control-arm fit of the ATE, that is, entropy balancing:

| **Fit of the linear logit** | **Estimand** | **Mean** | **SD** |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Maximum likelihood, HT | ATE | 1.477 | 0.153 |
| Maximum likelihood, Hájek | ATE | 0.862 | 0.088 |
| Calibration loss (HT $=$ Hájek) | ATE | 1.002 | 0.070 |
| Maximum likelihood, HT | ATT | 1.773 | 0.166 |
| Maximum likelihood, Hájek | ATT | 1.304 | 0.083 |
| Entropy balancing (HT $=$ Hájek) | ATT | 1.152 | 0.079 |

The maximum-likelihood rows reproduce the biases of @tbl-w6-lab2. The calibrated estimates are essentially unbiased for both estimands --- not because the score model has become right, but because the outcome is linear in $f(X)$ and the weights balance $f(X)$ exactly (to $10^{-7}$ in every replication), which is the situation of @prp-cal-dr and of its ATT analogue.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: High Dimension

With many covariates, @tan2020regularized adds a lasso penalty, minimizing $\ell_{\mathrm{CAL}}(\gamma) + \kappa\sum_j|\gamma_j|$. The first-order condition then becomes the box constraint $|n^{-1}\sum_i(T_i/\hat\pi_i - 1)f_{ij}| \le \kappa$ for every component $j$: balance within $\kappa$ rather than exact balance. Valid inference after regularization requires additional machinery --- a regularized fit of the outcome model as well --- which is beyond this chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Generalized Entropy Calibration

Both primal problems, @eq-w6-cal-primal and @eq-w6-att-primal, are instances of one calibration problem: minimize $\sum_{i\in S} G(\omega_i)$ subject to the balance constraint, for a strictly convex objective $G$ [@kwon2026generalized]. With $g = G'$, stationarity gives $\omega_i = g^{-1}(\lambda^\top f_i)$, and for the treated arm the dual objective is
$$F(\lambda) = \sum_{i\in S}\rho(\lambda^\top f_i) - \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda^\top f_i, \qquad \rho(\nu) = \nu\, g^{-1}(\nu) - G\{g^{-1}(\nu)\},$$
where $\rho$ is the convex conjugate of $G$ and $\rho' = g^{-1}$. The choice of $G$ fixes the form of the weights:

| **Objective** $G(\omega)$ | $\rho'(\nu)$ | **Weights** | **Use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\omega^2/2$ | $\nu$ | linear in $f$ | regression weights (Chapter 5) |
| $(\omega-1)\{\log(\omega-1)-1\}$ | $1 + \exp(\nu)$ | $1/\pi$ | ATE, treated arm (Tan's loss) |
| $\omega\log\omega - \omega$ | $\exp(\nu)$ | $\pi/(1-\pi)$ | ATT, controls (entropy balancing) |

The last two imply a logistic score. Conversely, any link $\pi$ defines $\rho' = 1/\pi$ and, through the conjugate, its own $G$. @prp-cal-dr and its ATT analogue hold for every $G$, because their proofs use only the constraint.
:::

## Overlap and Positivity {#sec-w6-overlap}

### Positivity and Strong Overlap {#sec-w6-positivity}

We must distinguish two conditions on the propensity score that play different roles in identification and inference.

::: {#def-positivity}
## Positivity (Weak Overlap)

The **positivity** condition --- also called *weak overlap* --- requires
$$0 < \pi(X) < 1 \quad \text{almost surely.}$$
Every unit has a positive probability of receiving either treatment or control --- more precisely, this holds for $P_X$-almost every covariate value.
:::

Together with unconfoundedness, positivity constitutes the *strong ignorability* of @rosenbaum1983central. Positivity is the condition needed for *identification*: without it, certain strata have no counterfactual information and the ATE is not nonparametrically identified.

::: {#def-strong-overlap}
## Strong Overlap

The **strong overlap** condition requires that there exists a positive constant $c \in (0, 1/2)$ such that
$$c \le \pi(X) \le 1 - c \quad \text{almost surely.}$$
:::

Strong overlap bounds the inverse weights $1/\pi(X)$ and $1/(1-\pi(X))$ uniformly away from infinity. Bounded weights do not bound the outcome, so strong overlap is only part of what $\sqrt{n}$ inference requires. For the known-score Horvitz--Thompson term, a useful sufficient moment condition is
$$\E\!\left[\frac{Y(1)^2}{\pi(X)} + \frac{Y(0)^2}{1 - \pi(X)}\right] < \infty,$$ {#eq-w6-ipw-moment}
which strong overlap together with $\E\{Y(t)^2\} < \infty$ guarantees. Together with finite outcome second moments and the regularity conditions of the estimator in use, strong overlap therefore supports the finite-variance, $\sqrt{n}$-consistent, asymptotically normal theory of later chapters (Chapter 12). It is sufficient for controlling the denominators, but it is not necessary: root-$n$ inference can survive under weaker, estimator-specific tail and moment conditions, provided the relevant influence function retains finite variance. Positivity alone permits identification but does not guarantee stable inference: when $\pi(X)$ approaches $0$ or $1$ in parts of the covariate space, the moment @eq-w6-ipw-moment can be infinite, the IPW weights blow up, a few units dominate, and the $\sqrt{n}$ rate fails even though the parameter is identified [@khan2010irregular]. Part 2 of the lab contains an example in which positivity holds, strong overlap fails, and the known-score HT estimator has infinite variance.

**Why positivity is necessary.** The identification formula
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E_X\bigl[\E[Y \mid T{=}1, X] - \E[Y \mid T{=}0, X]\bigr]$$
requires that both $\E[Y \mid T{=}1, X{=}x]$ and $\E[Y \mid T{=}0, X{=}x]$ be defined for $P_X$-almost all $x$ in the support of $X$. If $\pi(x) = 0$ on a set of covariate values of positive probability, then no treated units exist there, so $\E[Y \mid T{=}1, X{=}x]$ is undefined on that set and the ATE is not identified by adjustment without additional assumptions about $Y(1)$; similarly if $\pi(x) = 1$. Three grades should be kept apart: a violation on a $P_X$-null set is harmless; a violation on a set of positive mass is an identification failure; and a score that is small but strictly positive is not an identification failure at all, but an estimation problem --- limited information, extreme weights, and possibly infinite variance --- which is the subject of the rest of this section.

### Practical Consequences of Near-Violations {#sec-w6-near-violations}

Exact violations of overlap ($\pi(X) \in \{0,1\}$ on a set of positive mass) arise from eligibility criteria and deterministic treatment rules. *Near*-violations arise when one treatment is uncommon in parts of covariate space: some covariate strata have very few treated or control units, making the estimated propensity score close to $0$ or $1$.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Near-Overlap Problems

When $\hat\pi(X_i)$ is close to 0 or 1, the IPW weight $1/\hat\pi(X_i)$ or $1/(1 - \hat\pi(X_i))$ is very large. A small number of units with extreme weights can dominate the estimator, increasing variance dramatically. This is the *practical positivity violation* problem, distinct from the theoretical violation.
:::

Near-violations arise when a covariate is a near-perfect predictor of treatment, when the covariate distributions of treated and control groups barely overlap, or when the propensity score model is over-flexible and fits the treatment variable nearly perfectly in-sample. Severe lack of overlap is therefore not necessarily a model-fitting failure: it may reflect a genuine absence of comparable treated and control units in the target population, in which case the honest responses are those of the next two subsections --- trimming or re-targeting the estimand --- rather than model revision (cf. step 7 of the workflow in @sec-w6-design-workflow).

### Trimming Strategies {#sec-w6-trimming}

**Trimming by propensity score.** Restrict the analysis to units with estimated propensity scores in a prespecified interval $[\eta, 1-\eta]$ for some small $\eta > 0$. The estimand changes to the ATE in the trimmed subpopulation:
$$\tau_{\mathrm{trim}} = \E\bigl[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid \eta \le \pi(X) \le 1-\eta\bigr].$$
Note that the target population is defined by the *true* score $\pi(X)$, while the practical rule is applied with the estimated score $\hat\pi(X)$. With a consistent score estimate and negligible probability mass at the cutoffs, the two rules agree asymptotically; this does not make the uncertainty from estimating the rule negligible for inference, which must account for it [@yang2018asymptotic]. The choice of $\eta$ is a precision--target-population trade-off rather than a bias--variance trade-off in the usual sense: removing regions with extreme scores eliminates the largest weights, but it also discards observations and changes the estimand. The discrepancy between $\tau_{\mathrm{trim}}$ and the original ATE is a change of target, not a statistical bias relative to $\tau_{\mathrm{trim}}$, and the net variance need not decrease monotonically in $\eta$.

**The Crump et al. rule.** @crump2009dealing derive the subpopulation that minimizes the asymptotic variance of the ATE estimator under their criterion and assumptions; the simple symmetric interval $[\eta, 1-\eta]$ uses additional conditions, homoskedasticity among them. Cutoffs near $0.1$ often emerge from this calculation, so the fixed rule $\eta = 0.1$ --- trimming units with $\hat\pi(X) < 0.1$ or $\hat\pi(X) > 0.9$ --- is a common heuristic, though not an optimum for every estimator and outcome model.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Remark: Clipping the Score Is Not Trimming

Trimming restricts *both* arms to $\{\eta \le \pi(X) \le 1-\eta\}$ and estimates a causal effect in a stated subpopulation; @yang2018asymptotic replace the trimming indicator by a smooth inclusion weight so that inference can account for the estimated rule, and for a fixed smoothing parameter the smoothed target approximates the sharply trimmed one. A different and common practice is to *clip* the score, replacing $\pi(X)$ by $\tilde\pi(X) = \min\{\alpha_U, \max(\alpha_L, \pi(X))\}$ in the weights. Clipping is not a change of target population. In the population it multiplies treated outcomes by $\pi(X)/\tilde\pi(X)$ and control outcomes by $\{1-\pi(X)\}/\{1-\tilde\pi(X)\}$, two different reweightings of the covariate distribution, so the difference of the two normalized weighted means need not be a causal effect averaged over any common population.

A counterexample: let $X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$, $\pi(0) = 0.01$, $\pi(1) = 0.5$, and $Y(1) = Y(0) = X$, so that every individual effect is zero. Clip below at $\alpha_L = 0.1$, so $\tilde\pi(0) = 0.1$ and $\tilde\pi(1) = 0.5$. The probability limits of the two Hájek means are
$$\begin{aligned} \mu_{1,\mathrm{clip}} &= \frac{\E\{TY/\tilde\pi(X)\}}{\E\{T/\tilde\pi(X)\}} = \frac{0.5\cdot0.5/0.5}{0.5\cdot0.01/0.1 + 0.5\cdot0.5/0.5} = \frac{10}{11},\\ \mu_{0,\mathrm{clip}} &= \frac{\E\{(1-T)Y/(1-\tilde\pi(X))\}}{\E\{(1-T)/(1-\tilde\pi(X))\}} = \frac{0.5\cdot0.5/0.5}{0.5\cdot0.99/0.9 + 0.5\cdot0.5/0.5} = \frac{10}{21}, \end{aligned}$$
a difference of about $0.43$ with no treatment effect anywhere: the $x = 0$ treated units are reweighted by $0.1$, the $x = 0$ controls by $0.99/0.9$, so the two arms no longer average over the same distribution of $X$. Trim and say so, re-target and say so, or use bounded weights with a stated target; do not clip the score and report the result as the original estimand.
:::

### Re-targeting the Estimand to Avoid Overlap Failures {#sec-w6-retargeting}

Trimming restricts the population in order to preserve the ATE within a region of good overlap. An alternative, complementary response to overlap failure is to change which units the effect averages over: target the average treatment effect on a subset of the population (treated or control) for which the relevant side of positivity can be guaranteed.

**ATT (target the treated population).** The ATT averages $Y(1) - Y(0)$ over $X \mid T{=}1$ and therefore requires only that $\E[Y(0) \mid X = x]$ be identified where the treated population lives. The treated-covariate law is absolutely continuous with respect to $P_X$ with density proportional to the propensity score, $dP_{X \mid T=1} = \{\pi(x)/P(T{=}1)\}\, dP_X$, so treated-population mass concentrates on $\{x : \pi(x) > 0\}$; there the requirement reduces to $P(T{=}0 \mid X{=}x) > 0$, equivalently $\pi(x) < 1$. Hence, given consistency, $Y(0) \indep T \mid X$, and integrability, the remaining support condition for nonparametric identification by adjustment is that $\pi(X) < 1$ almost surely on the support of $X \mid T{=}1$. The ATT therefore tolerates regions with $\pi(x) = 0$ (no treated units are observed there in any case, so $X = x$ contributes nothing to the treated-population average); the ATT cannot tolerate regions inside the treated support where $\pi(x) = 1$ (no comparable controls).

**ATC (target the control population).** Symmetrically, given consistency, $Y(1) \indep T \mid X$, and integrability, the ATC averages $Y(1) - Y(0)$ over $X \mid T{=}0$ and is nonparametrically identified by adjustment if and only if $\pi(X) > 0$ almost surely on the support of $X \mid T{=}0$. The ATC tolerates regions where $\pi(x) = 1$ but not regions inside the control support where $\pi(x) = 0$. These equivalences are statements about the support conditions for nonparametric identification by adjustment, once consistency and the relevant arm-specific ignorability condition are in place; positivity by itself is never a complete identification condition. Additional outcome-model restrictions (e.g., a parametric model extrapolating into an unsupported region) could identify the same estimands under weaker support conditions, but then the model, not the data, supplies the answer.

**Practical rule, conditional on the question.** When overlap fails at covariate values where $\pi(X) \approx 0$ --- treated units are scarce or absent there --- and the treated population is the scientifically relevant one, the ATT is a more feasible target. When overlap fails where $\pi(X) \approx 1$ --- controls are scarce or absent --- the analogous consideration points to the ATC. When overlap fails on both sides, restrict to the trimmed-population estimand of the previous subsection, or use the overlap weights of the remark in @sec-w6-design-objectives. Re-targeting should answer a scientific question, not be an automatic response to whichever estimate is more stable; every remedy for an overlap failure changes the question, and the analysis must say which question is answered.

## Lab: Simulation Study of IPW and Matching Estimators {#sec-w6-lab}

This lab compares five estimators on a five-covariate data-generating process with treatment-effect heterogeneity. With five continuous confounders, direct stratification is infeasible, making propensity-score methods the natural choice. The estimators span two estimands: the ATE (targeted by the HT and Hájek IPW estimators) and the ATT (targeted by the ATT-IPW variants and by matching). Five questions drive the comparison:

1. How much variance does weight normalization save (Hájek over HT) for ATE estimation, and why does the baseline outcome mean matter?
2. Does the same variance problem afflict HT when targeting the ATT, and does Hájek normalization help as much?
3. Among estimators targeting the ATT, do IPW and matching agree on the target, and which is more efficient?
4. How large is the estimand gap between ATT and ATE, and which estimators reveal it?
5. How does replacing the true propensity score with a logistic estimate change bias and variance?

### Part 1: Correctly Specified Propensity Score {#sec-w6-lab-part1}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## DGP for Lab 6

Let $X_j \overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Normal}(0,1)$ for $j = 1, \ldots, 5$. All five covariates enter both the treatment mechanism and the outcome, so every $X_j$ is a genuine confounder. The true propensity score is
$$\pi(X) = \expit(-0.5 + 0.8X_1 + 0.5X_2 - 0.3X_3 + 0.2X_4 + 0.1X_5),$$ {#eq-w6-lab-ps}
giving marginal treatment probability $P(T{=}1) \approx 0.40$. The potential outcomes are
$$Y(t) \;=\; (1 + 0.5X_1)\cdot t \;+\; 8 + 0.8X_1 + 0.5X_2 + 0.4X_3 + 0.3X_4 + 0.2X_5 + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathrm{N}(0,1).$$ {#eq-w6-lab-po}
The CATE is $\tau(X) = Y(1) - Y(0) = 1 + 0.5X_1$. Because $\E[X_1] = 0$,
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E[1 + 0.5X_1] = 1.000 \quad (\text{exact}).$$ {#eq-w6-lab-ate}
Because $\pi(X)$ is increasing in $X_1$, treated units have higher $X_1$ on average, so $\E[X_1 \mid T{=}1] > 0$ and
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = \E[1 + 0.5X_1 \mid T{=}1] \approx 1.199 \quad (\text{Gaussian quadrature: } 1.19896).$$ {#eq-w6-lab-att}
The gap $\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} \approx 0.199$ reflects a selection effect: units most likely to be treated also tend to have larger individual treatment effects. The intercept $8$ in the outcome model represents a population baseline --- a health score in a generally healthy population. Treatment is generated as $T \mid X \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}\{\pi(X)\}$, the error satisfies $\varepsilon \indep (X, T)$, and units are sampled independently; strong ignorability therefore holds by construction. The observed outcome is $Y = Y(T)$.
:::

With five confounders, direct cell-by-cell stratification is infeasible: five continuous covariates cannot be coarsened without discarding information or requiring enormous samples. The propensity score reduces this five-dimensional adjustment to a scalar. The large baseline mean ($\E[Y(0)] = 8$) plays a distinct role: it amplifies the consequences of extreme IPW weights through @eq-w6-shift, making Hájek normalization strongly recommended in this setting rather than merely helpful, as the results below demonstrate.

**Estimators.** Five estimators are compared, each applied under both the true and estimated propensity score. The estimated score $\hat\pi(X)$ is obtained by logistic regression of $T$ on $(X_1, \ldots, X_5)$, which is correctly specified since the true logit is linear in all five covariates.

*Horvitz--Thompson ATE (HT-ATE)* and *Hájek ATE (HJ-ATE)* are the two forms of @sec-w6-ht-hajek, targeting the ATE. Raw inverse weights can be extreme when $\hat\pi(X_i)$ is near $0$ or $1$, and with $\E[Y(0)]=8$ the variance consequences are severe; normalizing by the empirical weight sum within each arm makes the estimate invariant to the outcome origin.

*Horvitz--Thompson ATT (HT-ATT)* and *Hájek ATT (HJ-ATT)* re-weight the **control** arm to look like the treated population while leaving the treated arm unchanged. Each control unit receives weight proportional to its *odds of treatment* $\hat\pi(X_i)/(1-\hat\pi(X_i))$: units whose covariates resemble the treated population receive large weight. For a control unit with $\hat\pi(X_i) = 0.95$ the weight is $19$; combined with a baseline outcome near $8$, this produces extreme variance --- in practice, even worse than HT-ATE. Because it divides by the random $n_1$, HT-ATT is not exactly unbiased in finite samples. The treated arm is already a simple mean and requires no normalization; the Hájek adjustment applies only to the control arm. HJ-ATT is the recommended default estimator for the ATT in practice.

*One-to-one nearest-neighbor matching with replacement (NNM)* pairs each treated unit with the control unit having the closest propensity score, with reuse allowed [@abadie2006large], and targets the ATT. Matching with replacement ensures every treated unit finds its closest control, avoiding the finite-sample "running out of good matches" problem that arises without replacement when the propensity score distribution is wide; by @eq-w6-nnm-weights it reweights the controls by their reuse counts.

**Results.** @tbl-w6-lab reports the Monte Carlo mean, bias, standard deviation, and RMSE across $B = 2{,}000$ replications at $n = 1{,}000$, seed `42`. Bias is computed relative to each estimator's own target: ATE $= 1.000$ for HT-ATE and HJ-ATE; ATT $\approx 1.199$ for HT-ATT, HJ-ATT, and NNM; entries are rounded from the simulation output, so a bias may differ in the last digit from the difference of the rounded mean and target. Monte Carlo standard errors of the reported means equal $\mathrm{SD}/\sqrt{B} \approx \mathrm{SD}/45$, here and in Part 2; reported biases should be read against this yardstick.

| **PS** | **Estimator** | **Estimand** | **Mean** | **Bias** | **SD** | **RMSE** |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Known | HT-ATE | ATE | 1.008 | $+$0.008 | 0.626 | 0.626 |
| | HJ-ATE | ATE | 1.003 | $+$0.003 | 0.145 | 0.145 |
| | HT-ATT | ATT | 1.184 | $-$0.016 | 0.725 | 0.725 |
| | HJ-ATT | ATT | 1.203 | $+$0.003 | 0.131 | 0.131 |
| | NNM | ATT | 1.207 | $+$0.008 | 0.130 | 0.130 |
| Estimated | HT-ATE | ATE | 0.998 | $-$0.002 | 0.194 | 0.194 |
| | HJ-ATE | ATE | 1.002 | $+$0.002 | 0.102 | 0.103 |
| | HT-ATT | ATT | 1.202 | $+$0.002 | 0.251 | 0.251 |
| | HJ-ATT | ATT | 1.202 | $+$0.002 | 0.101 | 0.101 |
| | NNM | ATT | 1.205 | $+$0.006 | 0.121 | 0.121 |

: Monte Carlo performance of five propensity-score estimators under known and estimated propensity scores. True ATE $= 1.000$ (exact); true ATT $\approx 1.199$. $n = 1{,}000$, $B = 2{,}000$ replications, seed `42`. {#tbl-w6-lab}

Five lessons stand out.

**1. Hájek normalization is strongly recommended for ATE estimation when outcomes are non-centered.** With the known propensity score, HT-ATE achieves SD $= 0.626$, while HJ-ATE achieves SD $= 0.145$ --- a **4.3-fold reduction in SD** from simply normalizing the weights. The mechanism is @eq-w6-shift: a unit with $\pi(X_i) = 0.05$ receives raw weight $1/0.05 = 20$; multiplied by an outcome near $\E[Y(0)] = 8$, its contribution to the HT sum is of order $160$. Variability in which units are extreme across samples enters HT through the fluctuation of $w_T - w_C$, amplified eightfold by the baseline, and inflates the HT standard deviation to more than half the true effect size; this, not variability in the treatment effect itself, is the dominant source of the HT variance here. The Hájek difference is exactly invariant to the shift, since each arm's self-normalized mean moves by $c$ and the shifts cancel. As the remark on normalization warns, this is a property of non-centered outcomes with fluctuating weight sums, not a universal variance ordering.

**2. HT-ATT is even more unstable; Hájek normalization is equally beneficial for ATT estimation.** With the known PS, HT-ATT achieves SD $= 0.725$, slightly *worse* than HT-ATE (SD $= 0.626$). The reason is structural: the ATT re-weights the control arm by the treatment odds $\pi(X)/(1-\pi(X))$. A control unit with $\pi(X) = 0.95$ receives an odds-ratio weight of $0.95/0.05 = 19$; combined with the large baseline outcome this is as explosive as the ATE inverse-probability weight. The apparent bias of $-0.016$ for HT-ATT is within one Monte Carlo standard error of $0.725/\sqrt{2000} \approx 0.016$ and should be attributed to simulation noise together with the finite-sample bias of dividing by the random $n_1$, not to inconsistency. HJ-ATT reduces SD to $0.131$ --- a **5.5-fold reduction in SD** --- confirming that Hájek normalization is not an ATE-specific fix but a general principle applicable whenever inverse-probability-style weights are used.

**3. HJ-ATT and NNM converge to the same target with nearly identical efficiency under the known score.** Under the known PS, HJ-ATT and NNM both target the ATT $\approx 1.199$ and achieve essentially the same standard deviation (0.131 vs. 0.130). This is the sharpest demonstration of the "two routes, one estimand" principle: IPW re-weights the full sample using the propensity score; matching discards some control units and retains only those nearest each treated unit on the propensity scale. Both are consistent for the ATT under strong ignorability, and at $n = 1{,}000$ they are virtually indistinguishable in efficiency. The practical implication is that the choice between IPW-ATT and matching can be made on secondary grounds --- interpretability, balance diagnostics, or computational cost --- rather than efficiency when the PS is known.

**4. The estimand gap between ATE and ATT is large and clearly revealed by the table.** The ATE estimators (HT-ATE, HJ-ATE) converge to $1.000$; the ATT estimators (HT-ATT, HJ-ATT, NNM) converge to $\approx 1.199$. The $0.199$ gap is not a bias --- it is a real difference in the estimands. High-$X_1$ units are more likely to be treated (@eq-w6-lab-ps) and have larger treatment effects (@eq-w6-lab-po); the treated subpopulation therefore benefits more than the full population average. A researcher who applies NNM and reports its output against the ATE benchmark of $1.000$ would conclude the estimator has $20\%$ bias; in fact it is unbiased for the correct target. Declaring the estimand before looking at any results is a non-negotiable discipline.

**5. The estimated PS collapses the HT variance and makes HJ-ATT the most precise ATT estimator in this design.** Under the estimated PS, the HT-ATE SD falls from $0.626$ to $0.194$ and the HT-ATT SD from $0.725$ to $0.251$: reductions of roughly two thirds in standard deviation, corresponding to variance reductions of about $90\%$ and $88\%$. This counterintuitive gain --- the *estimated* score outperforming the *true* one --- is @thm-estimated-score: the logistic model is exactly correct here and is fitted by maximum likelihood, so the likelihood equations $\sum_i \bigl(T_i - \hat\pi(X_i)\bigr)X_i = 0$ act as control variates and remove the component of the IPW sampling error correlated with the likelihood score vector. The Hájek-versus-HT ratios of Lessons 1 and 2 are correspondingly smaller with the estimated score (about $1.9$ and $2.5$), because part of what normalization removed is now removed by the fit. More strikingly, HJ-ATT with the estimated PS achieves SD $= 0.101$ --- below both NNM (SD $= 0.121$) and HT-ATT (SD $= 0.251$) and matching HJ-ATE (SD $= 0.102$) almost exactly. A properly normalized IPW estimator for the ATT is consistent --- though, as a ratio estimator, not exactly unbiased in finite samples --- and can be more precise than matching when the propensity score model is correct and well-estimated. This ranking is specific to the data-generating process and implementations compared: correct specification is not semiparametric efficiency, and there is no universal variance ordering between the two estimators.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The Estimand Must Be Chosen Before the Estimator

In this DGP, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = 1.000$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} \approx 1.199$. The gap arises because treatment status is correlated with the individual treatment effect: high-$X_1$ units are simultaneously more likely to be treated (@eq-w6-lab-ps) and more likely to benefit (@eq-w6-lab-po). This situation --- treatment-effect heterogeneity correlated with propensity for treatment [@imbens2015causal] --- is common in practice: individuals often select into treatment partly because they anticipate larger benefits.

IPW-ATE and HJ-ATE re-weight the full sample to represent the population; IPW-ATT and HJ-ATT re-weight only the control arm to represent the treated population; NNM directly pairs each treated unit with a similar control. All three ATT estimators target the same quantity via different mechanisms and deliver consistent results here. Choosing among them should be driven by the policy question (is the ATE or ATT the right estimand?) and by practical concerns about balance and model specification, not by which produces the larger or smaller point estimate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: What Part 1 Does Not Show

Part 1 uses a correctly specified logistic propensity model, which is the best-case scenario for IPW. In practice the true PS may be nonlinear, making correct logistic specification impossible with the predictors at hand. Part 2 below addresses exactly this setting. The doubly-robust AIPW estimator of Chapter 11 provides a complementary fix: it is consistent if *either* the PS model or the outcome model is correctly specified, offering robustness that neither pure IPW nor pure matching can achieve alone; @sec-w6-calibration shows how a calibrated fit of the score obtains the same protection at the fitting stage.
:::

### Part 2: Robustness to PS Model Misspecification {#sec-w6-lab-part2}

Part 1 established that under a correctly specified PS model, IPW and NNM are both consistent for their respective estimands, with HJ-ATT and NNM delivering similar efficiency. Part 2 breaks that assumption by introducing a *nonlinear* true propensity score that the standard logistic regression cannot capture.

**Modified DGP.** The outcome model is unchanged from @eq-w6-lab-po. The true propensity score now contains a quadratic term in $X_1$, and $X_2$ and $X_3$ do not affect treatment:
$$\pi^*(X) = \expit\{\ell(X)\}, \qquad \ell(X) = -0.5 + 0.8X_1 + 0.5X_1^2 + 0.2X_4 + 0.1X_5 .$$ {#eq-w6-lab-ps2}
The quadratic $0.5X_1^2$ means that both large positive *and* large negative values of $X_1$ increase the probability of treatment, creating a U-shaped propensity surface. Because $\E[X_1] = 0$ and the CATE is still $\tau(X) = 1 + 0.5X_1$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = 1.000$ exactly, unchanged. The ATT changes because the new PS shifts which units are treated:
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}}^* \approx 1.152 \quad (\text{Gaussian quadrature: } 1.15151).$$ {#eq-w6-lab-att2}
The *estimated* PS is still obtained by fitting a linear logistic regression of $T$ on $(X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4, X_5)$. This model is **misspecified**: it omits the $X_1^2$ term and includes $X_2$ and $X_3$, which do not appear in the true logit.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## This Design Has Positivity but Not Strong Overlap

Under @eq-w6-lab-ps2, $1/\{1 - \pi^*(X)\} = 1 + \exp\{\ell(X)\}$, and for $X_1 \sim \mathrm{N}(0,1)$ the quadratic coefficient $0.5$ exactly cancels the normal log-density:
$$\E\bigl\{\exp(0.5X_1^2 + 0.8X_1)\bigr\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp(0.8x)\,dx = \infty .$$
Since $\E\{Y(0)^2 \mid X\} \ge 1$, the moment condition @eq-w6-ipw-moment fails: $\E\{Y(0)^2/(1-\pi^*(X))\} = \infty$. Positivity holds --- $\pi^*(X) \in (0,1)$ for every $X$ --- but strong overlap does not, and the known-score HT-ATE estimator has *infinite* variance. The control contributions to the influence functions of the ATT and Hájek estimators also fail the finite-second-moment condition; a finite-sample Hájek estimate is bounded by the observed outcome range, but the usual finite-variance $\sqrt{n}$ approximation fails for it too.

The "True PS" rows of @tbl-w6-lab2 must be read accordingly: their Monte Carlo SDs are finite numbers that depend on the seed and can miss rare, extreme realizations. A rerun with a different seed gave $1.19$ and $2.24$ for the two HT rows instead of $0.824$ and $1.333$, and individual replications of HT-ATE can miss the target by more than $15$. Those SDs are not estimates of a finite theoretical standard deviation. This is a property of the stated model, not a coding error, and it is the concrete example promised in @def-strong-overlap: identification without stable inference.
:::

**Results.** @tbl-w6-lab2 reports the same five estimators as Part 1, now applied under the modified DGP. The "True PS" rows use $\pi^*(X)$ from @eq-w6-lab-ps2; the "Misspecified" rows use a linear logistic estimate $\hat\pi(X)$ that omits $X_1^2$. The probability limits of the misspecified-score IPW estimators can be computed by solving the population logistic score equations and integrating: $1.474$ (HT-ATE), $0.860$ (HJ-ATE), $1.776$ (HT-ATT), and $1.305$ (HJ-ATT), in agreement with the Monte Carlo means.

| **PS** | **Estimator** | **Estimand** | **Mean** | **Bias** | **SD** | **RMSE** |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| True | HT-ATE | ATE | 1.028 | $+$0.028 | 0.824 | 0.825 |
| | HJ-ATE | ATE | 1.013 | $+$0.013 | 0.152 | 0.152 |
| | HT-ATT | ATT | 1.186 | $+$0.034 | 1.333 | 1.333 |
| | HJ-ATT | ATT | 1.183 | $+$0.031 | 0.212 | 0.215 |
| | NNM | ATT | 1.178 | $+$0.026 | 0.175 | 0.177 |
| Misspecified | HT-ATE | ATE | 1.478 | $+$0.478 | 0.147 | 0.501 |
| | HJ-ATE | ATE | 0.861 | $-$0.139 | 0.087 | 0.164 |
| | HT-ATT | ATT | 1.780 | $+$0.628 | 0.162 | 0.649 |
| | HJ-ATT | ATT | 1.306 | $+$0.154 | 0.081 | 0.174 |
| | NNM | ATT | 1.172 | $+$0.020 | 0.138 | 0.139 |

: Part 2: Monte Carlo performance under a nonlinear true PS and a misspecified linear logistic estimate. True ATE $= 1.000$ (exact); true ATT $\approx 1.152$ (new DGP). $n = 1{,}000$, $B = 2{,}000$ replications, seed `42`. The true-PS SDs are seed-dependent finite-sample numbers (see the warning above). {#tbl-w6-lab2}

Three lessons complete the picture.

**6. A misspecified PS removes the consistency guarantee for IPW; normalization does not restore it.** Every IPW estimator using the misspecified score in this simulation is inconsistent: HT-ATE bias is $+0.478$, nearly half the true effect; HJ-ATE bias is $-0.139$; HT-ATT bias is $+0.628$; HJ-ATT bias is $+0.154$. Comparing these with the near-zero biases in the "True PS" rows makes clear that Hájek normalization does not generally restore consistency: a structurally wrong model produces structurally wrong weights. IPW consistency is generally tied to consistency of the PS estimator; the exceptions, such as a constant shift of the logit in the Hájek ATT estimator (@sec-w6-matching-misspec), are special. (The protection that *does* exist is specific and must be built in: @sec-w6-calibration fits the same linear logit so that the weights balance $X$ exactly, and because the outcome is linear in $X$ the resulting estimate is unbiased, $1.002$ with SD $0.070$, in @exm-cal-lab. Ordinary maximum likelihood provides no such protection here.)

Notice also that HJ-ATE and HT-ATE have biases in *opposite directions* ($-0.139$ vs $+0.478$): under misspecification the two estimators converge to different quantities, so normalization changes the limit even though it does not repair it. The mechanism is a multiplicative *level error* that HT inherits from misspecification. Recall the average inverse weights $w_T$ and $w_C$ from @sec-w6-ht-hajek, each of which converges to $1$ under a correctly specified PS. Under misspecification both can drift; in this DGP their limits are $w_T \approx 1.045$ and $w_C \approx 0.972$. The exact finite-sample relation is
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HJ}} = (w_T - 1)\,\hat\mu_1^{\mathrm{HJ}} - (w_C - 1)\,\hat\mu_0^{\mathrm{HJ}},$$
which evaluates to about $0.613$ in the limit; replacing the Hájek arm means by $\E[Y(1)] = 9$ and $\E[Y(0)] = 8$ gives the approximation $0.045 \times 9 + 0.028 \times 8 \approx 0.63$. Either way this accounts for essentially the entire gap between the two biases ($+0.478 - (-0.139) = +0.617$). With $\E[Y(0)] = 8$, even sub-five percent weight-sum errors translate into bias contributions of order $0.3$. What remains in HJ-ATE is a smaller *shape* error: the residual misweighting of the population that survives self-normalization. The level and shape errors are determined by different aspects of the misspecification --- the first by how far the average inverse weights drift from one, the second by how the misspecified weights re-weight the population --- so there is no reason for their signs to align.

**7. In this simulation, matching is far less biased than IPW under the misspecified score, and the prognostic score offers an explanation.** The NNM bias barely changes: $+0.026$ under the true PS versus $+0.020$ under the misspecified PS, and its RMSE is $0.139$. The linear logistic model, though wrong, retains the dominant linear dependence of treatment on $X_1$, $X_4$, and $X_5$, and in this design the matched pairs it produces remain close on the covariates that enter the outcome. That is an observation about this simulation, not a guarantee: close values of an arbitrary fitted scalar do not imply close covariate vectors or conditional exchangeability given that scalar, and a finite list of small standardized differences does not prove that the relevant population conditions hold. Before attributing a small bias to successful adjustment, assess balance on the outcome-relevant covariates and their transformations in the matched sample. @sec-w6-matching-misspec offers an explanation: after the outcome-only covariates $X_2$ and $X_3$ are set aside, the misspecified linear index is nearly a prognostic score for the remaining adjustment set $(X_1, X_4, X_5)$. The explanation is not an exact guarantee.

What matching needs can be stated precisely. For matching on a limiting scalar $b(X)$, a sufficient causal condition for the ATT is
$$\E\{Y(0) \mid b(X),\, T{=}1\} = \E\{Y(0) \mid b(X),\, T{=}0\},$$
together with the overlap, shrinking-discrepancy, moment, and regularity conditions of the warning on inference after matching. A correctly estimated propensity score is one way to obtain this condition, since the true score is a balancing score. By @lem-matching-valid, a misspecified score also provides it when it keeps the level sets of the true score (a wrong link, for instance) or of a prognostic score, even though it is not a correctly calibrated treatment probability. It does not provide it when the misspecification merges units with different scores and different prognoses, and then matching fails along with IPW (@exm-matching-misspec). The lesson is that the identifying condition for matching survives a larger class of misspecifications than the consistency of IPW does, because it depends on which units the score treats as alike rather than on the score's values. The finite-sample matches and any caliper still depend on the score's scale (@sec-w6-matching-misspec), and whether a given fit falls in that class is checked through balance after matching, not assumed. Related constructions in the literature should not be over-read: @yang2023multiply obtain a *multiply robust* matching estimator by matching on both propensity and prognostic scores (@sec-w6-prognostic) with a specific construction, which is a property of that estimator rather than a robustness guarantee for ordinary matching on one misspecified propensity score; @yang2016multilevel extend score matching and stratification to multi-level treatments.

**8. In this simulation, the efficiency ranking of matching and IPW reverses with model misspecification.** In Part 1 (correctly specified PS), HJ-ATT had a smaller empirical SD than NNM under the estimated PS ($0.101$ vs $0.121$). In Part 2 (misspecified PS), NNM has the smaller empirical RMSE ($0.139$ against $0.174$ for HJ-ATT), and the smaller bias. The comparison is summarized in @tbl-w6-comparison. These rankings are specific to the data-generating processes and implementations compared. The practical implication is that the efficiency advantage of IPW is contingent on the PS model being approximately correct. When there is reason to doubt the functional form of the propensity model --- for instance, when treatment is driven by a continuous covariate in a nonlinear way --- matching can be a more robust alternative, because it uses the fitted score only to decide which units are alike, not as a weight (@sec-w6-matching-misspec); whether this advantage materializes depends on whether the fitted score keeps the level sets of a balancing or a prognostic score, which balance on the outcome-relevant covariates after matching helps to assess.

|  | **Part 1: Correct PS model** |  | **Part 2: Misspecified PS model** |  |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Estimator** | Bias | RMSE | Bias | RMSE |
| HJ-ATT | $+0.002$ | $0.101$ | $+0.154$ | $0.174$ |
| NNM | $+0.006$ | $0.121$ | $+0.020$ | $0.139$ |

: Head-to-head comparison of HJ-ATT and NNM under correct vs. misspecified PS estimation (estimated PS column from each part). {#tbl-w6-comparison}

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## What the Lab Shows and Does Not Show

Both IPW and matching require causal identification assumptions and an adequate adjustment procedure. Ordinary IPW has a general consistency guarantee with a consistently estimated propensity score and suitable regularity; a misspecified score removes it, as the $+0.154$ HJ-ATT bias in Part 2 demonstrates. In Part 1, HJ-ATT has a smaller empirical SD than NNM with the estimated score; in Part 2, NNM has the smaller empirical RMSE. Neither ranking generalizes beyond the designs compared.

Matching keeps its identifying condition under the score misspecifications that keep the level sets of a balancing or a prognostic score (@lem-matching-valid), a larger class than IPW generally tolerates, and it is then consistent under the regularity conditions of the warning on inference after matching; but neither a small empirical bias in one simulation nor a finite set of balance diagnostics shows that a given fit belongs to that class: diagnostics support an assessment, they do not prove consistency. The favorable case must be examined through balance diagnostics on the matched sample --- including, where relevant, nonlinear transformations and interactions (@sec-w6-balance-diagnostics) --- not assumed.

Neither dominates unconditionally. The practical recommendation is to assess the plausibility of the PS model (e.g., via balance diagnostics after stratification or matching) before choosing between IPW and matching as the primary estimator, or to report both as a sensitivity check. Two further options widen the menu: the calibrated fit of @sec-w6-calibration, which protects IPW when the outcome is linear in the balanced covariates, and the augmented IPW estimator of Chapter 11, which is consistent if either the score or the outcome model is correct.
:::

## The Limits of Propensity Score Methods {#sec-w6-limits}

### The Untestable Assumption {#sec-w6-untestable}

The balancing property $T \indep X \mid \pi(X)$ (@thm-balance), the coarsest-balancing-score lemma, and the weighted-balance identities (@lem-weighted-balance) are properties of the observed treatment-assignment mechanism: they hold for any binary treatment and require no causal assumptions. The *causal* results of this chapter --- the Propensity Score Theorem, the IPW identification formula, the causal interpretation of matching --- additionally rest on the unconfoundedness assumption:
$$\bigl(Y(0),\, Y(1)\bigr) \;\indep\; T \;\Big|\; X,$$
together with consistency and the relevant positivity condition. Unconfoundedness requires that the observed pretreatment set $X$ be *sufficient for adjustment*. In graphical terms: $X$ blocks every back-door path from $T$ to $Y$. This does not require that every latent common cause itself be observed: an observed variable lying on a confounding path can block that path even when the common cause behind it is latent (Chapter 3). What is required is that every noncausal path be intercepted by the observed set --- and this can never be verified from the data alone. Balance on $X$ is necessary for a good design and says nothing about an unmeasured $U$.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Randomization versus Observational Adjustment

Random assignment *establishes* exchangeability for the assigned treatment --- conditional on the randomization strata, where those are used --- so that no back-door path exists and the interventional and observational distributions coincide. Observational adjustment, whether by stratification, weighting, or matching on a propensity score, *assumes* the relevant exchangeability condition: the analyst hopes that all confounders have been measured and included in $X$, but this can never be verified from the data alone. This distinction --- between identification secured by the study design and identification secured by a modeling assumption --- is one of the most important dividing lines in causal inference. Observational matching is often described as a "design" too, and the design stage of @sec-w6-design-workflow borrows the discipline of an experiment; what it cannot borrow is the guarantee.
:::

**Two complementary responses.** When unconfoundedness is in doubt, two distinct strategies are available and they answer different questions. *Sensitivity analysis* (Chapter 9) keeps the back-door framework but quantifies how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the conclusion: if the answer is "implausibly strong" the analysis is robust, whereas if the answer is "modest" the conclusion is fragile. The *instrumental variable* approach (Chapter 7) replaces the unconfoundedness assumption with a different set of identifying assumptions, exploiting an external source of variation in treatment that is independent of the unobserved treatment--outcome confounders. The hidden-confounding concern is thereby relocated, not eliminated: the instrument itself must be valid --- unconfounded with the outcome and excluded from affecting it directly. In short: sensitivity analysis preserves the original analysis and reports a robustness margin; instrumental variables substitute a different identifying assumption. The remainder of this section sketches the second route, since it is the topic of the next chapter.

### The Road to Instrumental Variables {#sec-w6-road-to-iv}

The limitation of back-door adjustment motivates the search for alternative identification strategies when unobserved confounders are present. One canonical alternative --- the one taken up next --- is the instrumental variable (IV), studied in Chapter 7. It is not the only one: front-door identification (Chapter 3) and sensitivity analysis with partial identification (Chapter 9) are others.

| **Strategy** | **Key assumption** | **Identification mechanism** |
|---|---|---|
| Back-door adjustment (propensity score) | Observed pretreatment set blocks all back-door paths | Condition on $X$ to block $T \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ |
| Instrumental variables | Some confounders may be unobserved | Exploit exogenous variation $Z \rightarrow T$ |

Back-door adjustment removes confounding by conditioning on observed variables. Instrumental variables take a different approach: instead of blocking the confounding path $T \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$, they isolate variation in $T$ induced by an external source $Z$ that is independent of $U$. Under additional IV assumptions, the ratio of the $Z$-induced change in $Y$ to the $Z$-induced change in $T$ --- the Wald estimator --- identifies a causal parameter. In the binary instrument and treatment setting, under the additional *monotonicity* (no-defiers) assumption, that parameter is the local average treatment effect (LATE) among compliers. This is derived formally in Chapter 7.

<figcaption>The instrumental variable design. The instrument Z shifts treatment T (relevance), is independent of the unobserved confounder U (exogeneity), and reaches the outcome Y only through T (exclusion). IV does not block the confounding path U &#8594; T, U &#8594; Y; it isolates the part of T's variation that is free of U.</figcaption>
